data.title: The Nvidia Story: Three Assessments Intersected
data.description:
Let’s pick up where we ended last week, when the details about Jensen Huang’s affairs and his subsequent ousting at Nvidia (NVDA) were just coming out.

Considering all that has happened in the intervening days, we need to go much deeper. This is one of the most important geopolitical developments of this year—and if it leads to a material and imminent worsening in US-China relations, one could make the argument that it is the most important development of the year.

THE SITUATION

Jensen Huang’s travails intersect three major geopolitical assessments I hold.

The first, which has received fair pushback from readers, is the long-term rivalry that is emerging between sovereign states and powerful tech companies. I argue that the Mag 7 and other tech companies that shape our daily lives are fundamentally expressions of a unipolar world. The worldview of these companies is ’90s-esque in their unbridled optimism and self-confidence in their mission. They see themselves as transcending politics because, in the ’90s, politics had been transcended. Communism lost, liberal democracy won, so let’s beat our missiles into iPhones and make memes.

The second is that the US-China relationship is on a trajectory of eventual conflict. If there is any bias in my work, it is that I think an eventual war between the US and China would be very bad for the world, for the US, and for China. I hope it doesn’t come to that. Hope isn’t analysis, however, and Washington and Beijing have fundamentally incoherent geopolitical imperatives. The US seeks to maintain its global primacy. China is not willing to kowtow and believes, at minimum, it should enjoy regional primacy. Yes, the US and Chinese economies are deeply interconnected. So were European economies on the eve of World War I. Graham Allison studied 16 historical cases of a rising power threatening to displace an established one; 12 ended in war.

The third is that the next two years will be relatively stable in US-China relations. Say what you will about President Donald Trump; he does not accept that the US and China should be rivals. He has worked hard to forge a constructive relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping. I have gone so far as to tell my clients to enjoy the next two years as the most stable in the US-China relationship we’ll see in the next 10.

The Nvidia story is a powerful confirmatory signal for assessments one and two. It is profoundly contradictory for the third.

1. The Jack Ma Parallel

What is happening to Jensen Huang and Nvidia is not much different than what happened to Chinese tech mogul Jack Ma and Alibaba back in 2020.

In October 2020, on the eve of an IPO for his fintech company Ant Group, Jack Ma went on stage in Shanghai and sharply criticized China’s banking system and government. Within two weeks, he’d been summoned for “regulatory talks” and his IPO was suspended. Months later, the Chinese government called China’s major tech companies’ leaders into a single room and told them essentially that unless they wanted to have the Jack Ma experience, they would do as the CPC—and specifically as Xi Jinping—said. China subsequently acquired shares with board seats in some of these companies, including Alibaba (BABA), and told them where they’d be allowed to sell, emphasizing the Chinese domestic market as their “mainstay.”

Is this really that different than the US government acquiring shares in companies it deems critical to its national security? In August 2025, Nvidia and AMD (AMD) agreed to pay the US government 15% of their revenue from Chinese sales of H20 AI chips and MI308 chips in exchange for export licenses. Jensen Huang is in trouble in part because he did not want to abide by US export controls (i.e., restrictions on where Nvidia would be allowed to sell its products). The only real difference is that in China, Jack Ma and others got on the wrong side of Xi Jinping; in the US, Jensen assumed a good relationship with President Trump would protect him. It did until the midterms, but now President Trump is weak, and the sharks smell blood in the water.

This is the beginning of a US government crackdown on tech. The state, to paraphrase Max Weber, is the monopoly on the legitimate use of force within given borders. The White House controls the men with guns. The men with data, capital, and technology possess extraordinary powers, but they must bend to the will of the men with guns.

2. The Next Boogeyman

The US has always needed boogeymen to define itself against—the British, the “Yellow Peril,” Japan, Nazi Germany, the Soviet Union. China is the next country on this list. It is also the first time in US history that its chosen rival is bigger. China lacks many things, to be sure. It cannot feed its own population, and it has grown dependent on energy imports. But at a very simple level, China has more people than the US. Neither the Soviet Union nor the combined forces of Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan could compete with the US on a demographic level.

They also could not compete with US manufacturing prowess. The US produced more merchant shipping tonnage in a single year than Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan produced in all of World War II combined. China is the world’s factory now; it accounts for 28–35% of global manufacturing output depending on your definition, and without Chinese rare earths and magnets and other components, the US economy will not work. The US is actively derisking its dependence on China, but this is a process that will take several years, if not decades. And the inconvenient truth is that today, the US is no less dependent on Chinese manufacturing than China is on access to Western markets and capital. This dependence only deepens US paranoia and drives it to manipulate markets away from China.

For most of its long history, China was content to be a dominant economic power within its own sphere of influence. But the growth of the Chinese population and the globalization of supply chains means that China is now dependent on trade and global supply chains. This is not your ancestors’ Middle Kingdom. This is a modern industrial state that must build a blue-water navy to defend its supply lines from enemies, whether pirates or US destroyers. In other words, China cannot defend its national security without creating the kind of military capabilities that Washington will interpret as a direct threat to its own primacy.

At a certain point, it is academic to argue whether China intends to pursue expansionist aims. Unless the CPC implodes (possible, if unlikely), the US and China will increasingly compete with and be suspicious of each other.

3. The Next Two Years

For all his talk of Make America Great Again, President Trump does not hold a fundamentalist belief in American primacy. President Trump has openly called the US-China relationship “the G2.” He sees China as a peer power with which he can make a deal. All his tariffs and machismo and posturing is about creating leverage to make a deal with China—not to fight China or assert US primacy.

Elements of President Trump’s own cabinet are not with him on this. Secretary of State and National Security Advisor Marco Rubio is a well-known China hawk and likely the source of the Jensen leaks. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has openly criticized Nvidia and China policy.

Moreover, being anti-China is one of the few true bipartisan positions left, and the Democrats seem to be relishing the Nvidia scandal for generating opportunities for hearings, aka political theater.

All of which leads me to the conclusion that my optimism about the next two years in the US-China relationship is broken. So far, what we’ve seen after the midterms:

  • Stephen Miller (as hardline a cabinet official as there is on China) elevated to Chief of Staff

  • Marco Rubio and Scott Bessent effectively kneecapping Trump’s friend Jensen Huang and his company Nvidia without so much as a peep from the president

  • In recent weeks, a steady drumbeat of quotes from officials like Bessent and US Trade Rep Jamieson Greer on China not living up to its prior trade and economic commitments.

We’ll see if President Trump is able to right things in his upcoming meeting with Xi—if he uses these developments to extract more concessions as part of his dealmaking tactics, or if he uses the China cudgel to his own benefit to buttress his abysmally low approval ratings. After all, he used anti-China invective to great effect in his first campaign back in 2015/2016. Time for some reruns.

Am I making a mountain out of a molehill? Perhaps we will know soon. But as George Friedman once told me, “Get excited, then get smart.” If you wait until something is obvious, you will always be behind. The only way to catch the one development in 10 that matters is to get excited about all 10, including the nine that end up not mattering. On this one, I’m excited.

MAP/CHART OF THE WEEK

BLIND SPOT

It has been a rough few weeks for Indonesia. The rupiah has fallen to record lows on the dollar. MSCI warned last month that the country’s emerging-market status was in jeopardy, leading to the benchmark Jakarta index tumbling ~15% (from which it still has not recovered). Last week, Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka—son of former President Joko Widodo (aka Jokowi)—resigned after questions about his educational credentials led to threats of impeachment.

Gibran’s joining the ticket with current Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto was seen as a positive note of stability in the country’s politics, but that is gone now. Prabowo is instead consolidating power, removing Jokowi allies from positions of power. Prabowo’s tenure has seen attacks on central bank independence, turmoil in the finance ministry, off-budget populist spending programs, and doubts about the governance of the country’s new sovereign wealth fund. Widespread Gen-Z/student protests erupted in August and September over inflation and governance issues but have fizzled (for now).

Indonesia is the fourth most populous nation in the world at ~300 million people. Its demographics are (relatively) strong. It is the world’s most populous Muslim-majority nation, and its relationship with Islam is famously moderate and pluralistic. The country sits astride critical maritime trade corridors. It contains impressive reserves of critical resources like nickel and copper, and is a major coal producer. In a multipolar world, Indonesia should be a rising power.

And yet the country seems determined to squander its potential. Some of this is understandable—Indonesia is a unique archipelagic nation, home to many different ethnic groups and languages. But Jokowi’s presidency seemed to be a break from the past, suggesting to optimistic observers that Indonesia might be on the cusp of transcending its differences, of utilizing its diversity as a strength rather than as something that was holding it back. But it turns out Prabowo, who has deep family ties to the authoritarian regime of Suharto and lived in self-imposed exile for years due to allegations over his role in the kidnapping and torture of pro-democracy activists, is reverting to form, attempting to centralize power rather than build coalitions.

data.title: Stock Report: Nippon Electric Gas Could Gain 15.10% Next Year
data.description:
Nippon Electric Glass Co., Ltd. was founded in 1944 and is headquartered in Otsu, Japan. NPEGF manufactures and sells specialty glass products and glassmaking machinery.

Three key data points gauge NPEGF (or any dividend-paying equity):

(1) Price
(2) Dividends
(3) Returns

Those three keys also indicate how much money a shareholder has made, is making, and might make.

NPEGF Price

Nippon Electric Glass’s single-share price fell $3.88 (or 11.73%) in the past year, from $33.08 to $29.20.

However, NPEGF’s three-year price progression from $19.03 in November 2023 to $29.20 in November 2026 showed an average annual gain of $3.39.

I’ll use that annual estimate of $3.39 to calculate returns after I discuss NPEGF dividends.

NPEGF Dividends

Nippon Electric Glass has paid variable semi-annual dividends since July 1987.

The next semi-annual dividend, estimated at $0.5024 per share, is expected to pay out in March to shareholders of record December 31st. The forward-looking annual dividend of $1.021 yields 3.50% (per Wednesday’s opening market report).

NPEGF Returns

Putting it all together, as of November 18th, a possible Nippon Electric Glass gross gain of $4.41 per share was projected.

To get there, our $3.39 per share estimated potential annual price gain was added to the $1.021 presumed forward-looking annual dividend to make that $4.41 gross gain.

A $1,000 investment in Nippon Electric Glass at Wednesday’s $29.20 opening price would buy about 34.25 shares, bringing the hypothetical $4.41 per-share gross gain to $151.03 for the coming year, or 15.10%.

By the way, one dividend dogcatcher guideline is to only buy initial shares of a dividend stock that pay an annual dividend (from $1,000 invested) that is more than the cost of one share.

NPEGF’s projected annual dividend from $1K invested is $34.97, and that annual dividend proves to be nearly 1.20 times its Wednesday $29.20 single-share opening price (or $5.77 more).

The exact track of Nippon Electric Glass’s future share price and dividend will entirely be determined by market action and company finances.

Remember, the best way to track stock performance and dividend payments is through direct ownership of company shares.

data.title: EU Lawmakers, States Agree To 2-Year Delay To Methane Reporting Rules
data.description:
Lawmakers in the European Parliament and EU Member States announced that they reached a provisional agreement to postpone methane monitoring and reporting rules for oil, gas and coal importers by two years, supporting an EU Commission proposal aimed at avoiding adding pressure to the EU’s security of energy supply.

While extending the delay beyond the Commission’s initial one-year proposal, the agreement marks a compromise between Parliament’s and the European Council’s positions going into negotiations of a 3-year and 1-year postponement, respectively.

Rapid reduction in methane emissions is seen as one of the most effective near-term actions that can be taken to help achieve the global climate goal to limit warming to 1.5°C. Methane is an extremely potent greenhouse gas (GHG), with as much as 80x the warming power of CO2, and oil and gas facilities are among the largest industrial sources of methane emissions.

The EU adopted a new law in 2024 setting rules for measuring, reporting and verifying methane emissions, for finding and repairing leaks, and for limiting venting and flaring, representing the world’s first comprehensive legislation to regulate methane emissions related to imports of oil, gas and coal.

The requirements for monitoring, reporting and verification for natural gas, oil and coal importers are currently set to begin in 2028, but in October the Commission proposed a one-year delay, citing a need to help avoid additional pressures on the security of supply of imported fossil fuels in the current geopolitical context.

Parliament adopted its negotiating position in October, proposing to extend the delay to 2031, noting that importers have warned that they may not be able to secure enough compliant supplies, with energy markets already strained. Council’s position aligned with the Commission’s 1-year delay, but added a requirement for the Commission to assess by September 30, 2027 whether the necessary elements for the implementation of the reporting obligations are met, including a sufficient number of third-party verifiers to assess the conformity of the emission reports, and whether there are in place EU implementing rules on transferring information about methane emissions between producers and importers, as well as on equivalent third-party verification and monitoring procedures in third countries.

The compromise agreement, which still requires endorsement by Parliament and the Council, would delay the rules by 2 years, with monitoring, reporting and verification obligations for natural gas, crude oil and coal importers beginning in January 2029, while also maintaining the Council’s requirements, including requiring the Commission to review the effective implementation of the methane regulation by the beginning of January 2028.

data.title: Different Pages
data.description:
old hasn’t been able to catch a break lately, and since its latest failed attempt to get back above the 50-DMA on 11/10, prices have pulled back more than 10%, pushing it further into the red for the year. As a reminder, gold was up over 20% YTD earlier this year.

Recent action has been especially painful for gold, and based on current levels, it is now trading down more than 20% in just the last three months. Earlier this year, gold’s three-month decline from its peak came close to 20% but fell just short. If current levels hold, it would be the first decline of that magnitude since June 2013.

Gold has been considered a store of value for thousands of years, so to see a decline of this magnitude is shocking. As the final chart illustrates, there have only been a handful of prior occurrences in the last 50+ years when it declined by at least 20% in three months.

In the short run, any number of factors could explain a sharp drop in gold, but with such a sustained and persistent decline, the market and the Fed seem to be on different pages with regard to inflation. Fed officials have expressed concerns about being behind the inflation curve, but with gold deflating at the fastest rate in more than a decade, the market would argue otherwise.

data.title: Armageddon ’26?
data.description:
Markets may be imitating Armageddon ’08 (AKA “the Great Financial Crisis” per the media)

They called it the Great Financial Crisis or the Great Recession. But there was nothing great about it. It was the market’s natural unwinding of years of inflationary inputs from the Greenspan Fed and the commercial banking industry’s excesses in lending to anything with a pulse and a mouth to utter “gimme!”

A credit bubble of immense and dangerous proportions.

I immediately dubbed it Armageddon ’08 in the then brand spanking new NFTRH because that is what it was, a final reckoning of good (natural market functioning) vs. evil (remote controlled markets managed by monetary socialists in favor of the financial services industry).

In today’s reckoning, ‘good’ seeks not to unwind commercial credit but instead, official (government/Fed) credit and debt. The kind of $40T plus in leverage that has maintained a rising GDP but and even better rising Debt-to-GDP.

At 121% debt leverage, the word “unsustainable” is way too mild. This train must be stopped!

And stop it they will, in my opinion. Because Fed and Treasury policymakers will not be able to manufacture the next inflation phase without a massive decline in today’s inflation fears, which we addressed in NFTRH last weekend.

So what gives here? Listen, I have been going on about the goddamn inflation in the headlines not really being inflation, and it isn’t. It’s a presidential administration circumventing a toothless and sycophantic congress, willy nilly imposing global tariffs and deciding to go to war with a nation that has a choke hold on a body of water that is critical to oil/energy prices, which are critical to the prices of pretty much everything else.

That is not inflation. It is elevated prices due to Trump’s poor decision making. Yes, I am being kind here.

The United States went to war and now it, and the rest of the world deal with the consequences. That is NOT inflation. Inflation was when Greenspan/Bush oversaw a bubble in credit, when Bernanke inflicted QE and 7 years of ZIRP upon the macro under Obama. When Powell panicked and printed a bailout and eventually another bull market in 2020, under Donald John Trump.

Inflation is at its creation, only ever a monetary thing.

Inflation is how they will eventually reduce the debt. We all know this. They will attempt to inflate it away. To do that, the US dollar has got to be loaded with asset market refugees.

And speaking of Armageddon, the 2 Horsemen of the Macro Liquidity Apocalypse are riding together. When the Gold/Silver ratio and USD rise impulsively in unison, that is anti-liquidity to the max as USD receives risk-off liquidity and gold also receives it from money that will be proven smart in the future. But in the present gold will decline less than other assets, including silver, commodities, and if our Armageddon script is on target, eventually stocks.

Bessent and Warsh are not dumb enough (I don’t think) to believe that we have an inflation problem today. Nor is this guy, who’s out jawboning public perceptions:

Since the 30yr Treasury yield Continuum made its upside breakout (and secular trend change) in 2022 our job has been to interpret the new macro and its coming phases.

This year Bessent and Warsh tag-teamed the bond market to create upside (and anti-inflationary/dollar-supportive) pressure on short-term yields, while limiting the downside and even helping spur a hard pullback in long-term yields. This did not resolve to a Goldilocks environment as I had originally thought might conveniently come about in the run up to the mid-term elections. Ref:

Operation Twist 2.0? Bessent & Warsh Work the Yield Curve (Aug. 28)

Now, any remaining vestiges of a pleasant economy (like a yield curve undecided between Goldilocks and a deflationary steepening) are dissipating. It is pretty obvious that the yield curve is going to resolve this volatile sideways move.

If it resolves down, the economy and risk markets stand a chance to negate the main premise of this article (broad markets following gold, silver and commodities down). If the curve resolves upward into a steepening, it is likely to do so under deflationary pressure (a ‘bull steepener’ in bonds), which I believe the likes of Mr. Waller and his jawbone above are getting at.

If this is Armageddon ’26 the broad stock market indexes will follow the precious metals, and AI datacenter trades like semiconductors and now copper and other AI datacenter hype into the hopper.

The point of this article, however, is not just Armageddon. Although, by the way, evil always wins this battle. It will win when it manufactures the next inflation problem with the public once again begging for it (as they did in 2001, 2008 and 2020. That is the rude irony. The evil irony. The thing that the public abhors now is exactly the thing it will be begging for if markets implode, 2008 or even 2020 style.

The vampire must be invited into your house. Enough of the public must be demanding inflation (printing, money supply increases, bailouts, etc.) because this is a cynical and sensitive blood sucker. It must feel wanted.

Opportunity would come from such a terrifying disaster. Q4, 2008 was terrifying as I bought gold stocks at HUI 250, had my hands severed by catching those falling knives, and used the last of my powder to buy at HUI 150, thankfully the bottom. It worked fabulously well. It happened again to a less dramatic degree in 2020.

We are watching and gauging the process because the precious metals lead. Gold > Miners > Silver or a similar progression, to the downside or upside. I am trying to be a patient buyer (currently sitting on my hands) until the stock market gives up and puts on a classic tank job that even the public notices. That would be a trigger to get very interested in quality gold stocks, first.

Disclaimer: I hold one gold exploration stock after taking profits (on balance) on most gold stock positions and being a little too patient and taking losses on others for a moderate portfolio draw down over the last several weeks. But cash and short-term Treasury equivalents have been the primary positions held and advised for months in NFTRH.

data.title: Silver Tests 4500 As Palladium Challenges Long-Term Support
data.description:
Thursday's markets are giving us another opportunity to revisit the technical scenarios we've been following.

Gold and copper have reached previously identified downside targets, the U.S. dollar is fighting to preserve its latest bullish gains, and platinum is approaching another important Fibonacci target.

Meanwhile, silver has slipped beneath the psychological 4500 barrier, and palladium is challenging several significant support levels.

The interesting part? Many of the conditions we identified earlier remain just as relevant today.

Let's focus on two precious metals facing particularly important tests.

Silver (SI.F) - The Battle for 4500 Continues

Wednesday's closing candle left silver buyers with a problem.

Although they managed to finish the session above the psychological 4500 barrier, the close below the 173.2% Fibonacci extension at 4553.37 kept the bearish outlook intact.

Thursday's buyers attempted to recover that Fibonacci resistance, but their efforts proved short-lived. Sellers regained control and pushed silver to 4443.50, once again breaking beneath 4500 intraday.

And that brings us directly to yesterday's warning:

“(…) Could the Decline Continue?

A confirmed daily close below 4500 would strengthen the bearish case for another decline.

The next clearly identified technical objective on our daily chart lies around 4250-4257, where the 200% Fibonacci extension at 4256.83 provides potential support.(…)”

That scenario remains fully relevant.

Daily Takeaway: Silver has fallen below 4500 intraday, bringing the next potential target at 4250-4257 back into focus.

Bottom Line: sellers retain the advantage, but today's closing price will determine whether the latest breakdown receives confirmation.

Palladium (PA.F) - Long-Term Support Comes Under Attack

Monday's warning is now playing out on Thursday's chart. Let's revisit what we wrote back then in Premium Lab Note:

“(…) failure to defend the fresh bullish gap would bring the lower boundary of the red declining channel (…) back into focus.

A confirmed breakdown below that line could expose the long-term green support (…), based on the March and June lows. (…)”

Well, look where palladium is now.

Thursday's decline has carried prices below the lower boundary of the red declining channel, the long-term green support line, and the November low at 922. That's a significant bearish development - although today's daily close must still confirm these latest breakdowns.

Where Could the Bears Strike Next?

If sellers maintain their advantage, the next downside objectives are:

  • 900: the psychological barrier

  • around 882: the 127.2% Fibonacci extension, if sellers overcome 900.

What could invalidate the latest bearish signals?

A recovery and daily close above 958 would challenge Thursday's breakdowns and weaken the immediate bearish case. Until then, sellers have stronger technical arguments for continuing their advance.

Daily Takeaway: three important support barriers have been breached intraday, with 900 and 882 becoming the next conditional downside objectives.

Bottom Line: Palladium's bearish structure has deteriorated further, but the final daily close remains essential.

What About the Other Four Markets?

U.S. Dollar - The Bulls Fight Back

A fresh bearish gap initially threatened the dollar's latest advance, but buyers responded with another push toward new local highs. Now two opposing gaps are helping define the next important technical battle.

Gold - Another Downside Target Achieved

Gold has fulfilled another consolidation-based bearish projection, but sellers aren't showing much interest in stopping. With additional Fibonacci support levels approaching, the next stages of the correction are coming into focus.

Platinum - Another Target Within Reach

Platinum's confirmed breakdown beneath its declining channel continues to influence the market. Sellers have approached another Fibonacci objective, leaving buyers with an increasingly difficult technical challenge.

Copper - The Fibonacci Combination Under Pressure

Copper has reached an important support zone formed by two Fibonacci levels. A subsequent recovery attempt has struggled, raising the possibility of another test and potentially a deeper decline if support fails. 

Final Thought - Let the Market Confirm the Next Chapter

Technical projections give us potential destinations while price action tells us whether the market is moving toward them. Nevertheless, reaching a target doesn't automatically guarantee another move in the same direction. That's why we keep returning to the conditions that matter.

An intraday breakout can be meaningful, but a confirmed closing price provides stronger evidence.

With several markets testing important technical boundaries, there's plenty to watch.

data.title: Gold Down, Silver Down: No Reason To Panic
data.description:
Having just come off nine days of gold presentations in two languages, three cities and even more price swings, it’s time for a reality check on the price action in gold and silver, both of which have reached bear territory this year, with silver falling twice as fast.

Are we worried?

No. We are buying.

Time Not Timing

For those speculators agnostically trading the metals long or short in a market-timing maze of buy/sell signals, nothing explained below will resonate. 

This is because we are buyers rather than traders of precious metals. 

We see gold and silver as monetary metals confronting a monetary sea change in which the compounding impact of inflation will reduce fiat currency purchasing power by at least 70% in the next decade. 

In this hard light of wealth preservation, our focus is time, not timing. And our store of value, confirmed by centuries, is real money not paper currencies.

And time, as the song says, is on our side.

Many, of course, will see this as apologetics from sell-side “gold bugs.”  

But for those who understand history, math and risk management, the case for precious metals is as obvious today as a cavity to a dentist. 

Gold’s longer-term trajectory is now mathematically assured by its inverse relationship to paper currencies. In this light, the price falls of 2026 are effectively a buyer’s gift.

Peak Lunacy, Not Peak Gold

We are very far from peak gold, but simultaneously at the apex of what the American bond king, Jeffrey Gundlach, described as “peak lunacy.”

In fact (and coming as no surprise to any familiar with my obsession with credit markets), if one seeks conviction in gold, the signals begin in those boring and hence ignored credit markets. 

And yes, the objective lunacy of the global credit profile is staggering.

Private Credit’s Pain Delay

As warned earlier this year, the “weapons of mass destruction” lurking within the private credit minefield have only grown more threatening. 

These private credit books are held by a wide range of insurance, annuity and pension funds holding the very same folio of loans yet at extremely diverse valuations. 

From a perfect par score of 100, for example, the same book of loans marked by entity “X” at 90 will be marked by entity “Y” at 20 or 30. Based on real math, the entire private credit space deserves little more than a triple-C rating (with scores at 60), and that’s being very generous.

This valuation disparity is partly due to the fact that ratings agencies with staffs of thirty can not effectively underwrite thousands of credits. 

But the darker truth is that these PC funds are just lying about their homemade valuations and hoping for a miracle to save them. This explains why investors in their gated funds can only get 5% of their money out per quarter. 

Their pain cannot be avoided, merely postponed. 

Even More Lunacy: From Private Equity to AI

Then there is private equity, another credit bug looking for a windshield. 

Its prior LBO (levered buyout) model succeeded on a premise of cheap credit with rates at 0% to 2%. Those days and rates are over, yet an entire generation of PE sponsors, who have never seen rates above 5%, still pretend to be what they once were.

Far worse, of course, is the greatest misallocation of capital and credit in the history of capital markets, namely the AI Nirvana-to-Nightmare template.

Not only have five tech hyper-scalers (who account for 90% of the S&P’s earnings) grossly over-invested $1.1 trillion in AI CAPEX, but they’ve also squandered an additional $3T in off-balance-sheet debt in two AI monopolies (OpenAI and Anthropic), showing respective operating losses of $8B and $14B.

The quarter-over-quarter margins for these two un-moated tech fantasies are falling, not rising. In short, AI’s best days have passed, yet the market prices its future for perfection.

No one believes the ratings on these credits, the spreads of which are widening. Soon, this credit boom will mathematically morph into yet another credit bust as investors revolt, credit tanks and defaults peak in a reckoning reminiscent of 2008.

Meanwhile, as everyone from CoreWeave to Google is burning through cash and competing for your data center sucker-money, the markets are turning a blind eye to default risk whose objective levels surpass the subprime crisis (and mis-ratings) of the GFC.

Ultimate Lunacy – Sovereign Debt

But if such lunacy in private credits wasn’t scary enough, just look at government debt. In the last 25 years, global government debt has skyrocketed by >5X from $21T to $115T. 

What’s worse is that the cost of that debt has reached decade highs, as evidenced by the decade highs in sovereign bond yields. 

And as for the home of the world’s reserve currency, it spends over $7.5T per year against an income of just $5T. 

Just six years ago, U.S. public debt was $23T, and the cost of borrowing was 0.5%.

Today, that debt is over $40T, and the cost of borrowing is above 5%. 

Do the math…

Very soon, Uncle Sam’s only options will be constructive default or bazooka money, either of which will send precious metals well beyond their prior highs of January 2026.

Chasing Yield, Ignoring Disaster

Despite these warnings, patterns and patient signals, today’s desperate debt issuers and equally desperate yield-chasers are thinking only of timing their next trade rather than contemplating these historical risks.

They see $1.9T of 2026 investment-grade bond issuance with coupons as high as 6% to 8%; they see USTs offering 5% to 6% yield. And they tell themselves this “sure beats a yield-less pet rock.”

Such optimized herd-thinking is nothing new. As the institutional “smart money” goes further out on the risk branch looking for yield and laughing at gold to make their annual performance bonus, what they are refusing to see would be almost comical, if it was not otherwise so tragic.

In particular, this lunatic market has three key blind spots.

data.title: Is Copper Signaling A Recession… Or Is China Cornering The Metal?
data.description:
Copper fell for a fifth straight session yesterday, dropping as much as 5.6% on the London Metal Exchange to a seven-month low. It is now 14% below the record it set in September. Eleven of the largest copper miners in the world have lost $141 billion in market value in a month, $68 billion of it in the past week. Stan Druckenmiller, who spent the past two years as the most prominent backer of the AI copper trade, said on Tuesday that he is short.

That is the paper market. Now look at the physical one.

On the same day copper hit its low in London, the premium Chinese buyers pay to import physical metal hit a record $360 a tonne. In September it was under $100. Copper stocks in Shanghai warehouses fell 18% last week to 27,642 tonnes, the lowest since December 2023. The fee smelters charge to process ore has gone to a record negative $247 a tonne, which means smelters are now paying miners for the privilege of treating their concentrate, because there is not enough ore to go around. Chile, which produces a quarter of the world’s copper, is on track for its weakest year of output in 23 years.

So on Wednesday the price of copper on paper said recession, and the price of copper in a warehouse said shortage, and the two moved in opposite directions on the same afternoon.

I wrote last week about the two-price system the Pentagon created for rare earths, a China price and a war price, with Washington guaranteeing the second one. Copper now has two prices too. Nobody in Washington set them. The market did, and the gap between them is the most useful thing I can show you this week.

The paper price is a vote on the Fed. Copper is the most financialized industrial metal there is, and over the past two years it became a proxy for the AI buildout. Hedge funds bought copper futures the way they bought Nvidia, as a bet on data center construction. Over the past month that bet unwound. The dollar is at a 19-month high. The Fed is going to hike on December 9. Financing costs are rising, the AI complex has been deleveraging since the margin call on November 5, and the tariff trade that pulled nearly a million tonnes of metal into U.S. warehouses is fading as the odds of refined copper tariffs drop. When Druckenmiller says he is “really alert to the fact that the second half of ’27 could be economically disappointing,” that is the trade he is describing: a Fed mistake, a slowdown, and a metal that fell by half in 2008 and by a quarter or more in 2015 when the last two slowdowns hit.

He may be right about the Fed. I think he is. But the physical market is voting on something else.

The physical price is a vote on the war. China is paying a record premium to pull copper out of a market that paper traders are dumping. A buyer that expects a recession waits for lower prices. A buyer that pays a record premium into a falling market wants the metal more than it cares about the price, and China wants copper for the same reason the Pentagon wanted dysprosium: it is a strategic asset in a gray-zone war, and whoever holds the physical supply holds the chokepoint. The exchange stocks tell the story. About 85% of the world’s exchange-monitored copper, roughly 1.09 million tonnes, is sitting in U.S. warehouses, pulled there by the tariff trade. Shanghai is nearly empty. The metal went west on paper and China is paying up to bring it back east in fact.

And the supply side has broken while everyone was watching the AI trade. A negative treatment charge is the rarest signal in the copper market. It means smelting capacity, most of it in China, is so far ahead of mine supply that smelters are competing for ore at a loss. Chile’s decline is not a one-year problem; its deposits are aging, its grades are falling, and its biggest mines depend on imported sulfuric acid. The Global X report this week put the number on the other side of the ledger: a single one-gigawatt AI data center needs about 27,200 tonnes of copper, demand for copper, lithium and rare earths could exceed mined supply by 17% to 22% by 2035, and a new mine takes 10 to 18 years to build.

Put it together. The paper market is pricing a slowdown that the Fed may well cause. The physical market is pricing a shortage that the geology has already caused. Both can be right for a while, and they cannot be right for long, because copper gets used. At some point a data center, a grid operator or a missile plant needs the metal, and it does not care what the futures curve thinks about the Fed.

This is what makes copper different from the AI stocks that dragged it down. Nvidia can fall 20% and nothing in the physical world changes. Copper can fall 20% and the shortage gets worse, because every dollar the price drops is a mine expansion that doesn’t get financed, in a world where the mines already take 15 years. Druckenmiller is betting that the paper price pulls the physical price down. The Chinese premium is a bet that the physical price pulls the paper price up. Only one of those bidders has a government behind it, and it isn’t the hedge funds.

What to do with it.

First, do not buy the dip in the miners yet. The paper market is deleveraging, the Fed is three weeks from a hike, and a market that has fallen five days in a row into a dollar at 19-month highs can fall five more. The names that lost $141 billion in a month can lose more. Druckenmiller’s timing on the macro has been better than almost anyone’s for 40 years, and the slowdown he is describing is real. Let the paper price finish voting.

Second, watch the premium, not the price. The Chinese import premium is the one number that tells you whether the physical bid is holding. As long as it stays above $200 a tonne while the paper price falls, the gap is widening, and a widening gap between a price and its underlying resolves violently. If the premium collapses back under $100, China has stopped buying and Druckenmiller wins outright.

Third, understand what you are watching. Three weeks ago it was rare earths, with the Pentagon putting a floor under the war price. Last week it was patches and exploits. This week it is copper, with China putting a floor under the war price with its own purchases while Western funds sell. The pattern is the same every time. Strategic assets get repriced by the side that needs them most, and the side that needs them most is never the one trading the futures.

I expect that by the end of the first quarter of 2027, LME copper trades back above $14,000 a tonne, and the gap between the paper price and the Chinese premium closes with the paper price rising rather than the premium falling. What would make me wrong: the import premium falling below $150 a tonne, which would mean Chinese demand has actually stalled, or a Fed hiking cycle that pushes the dollar high enough to break emerging-market demand entirely. The first would surprise me. The second is the real risk, and it is why I would wait for the Fed before buying anything.

Druckenmiller sold copper and bought gold miners. Read that as a vote on the Fed. China sold nothing and paid a record premium. Read that as a vote on the war. In a wartime economy, the second vote is the one that gets honored.

But honor it later. The thing to respect right now is the paper market, because the paper market is where crashes start. Copper is the most economically sensitive asset there is, and it has just fallen five days in a row into a Fed hike, a dollar at a 19-month high, and an AI complex that has been deleveraging since November 5. The last two times copper broke like this with the Fed tightening, 2008 and 2018, stocks followed within months. That is the setup Druckenmiller is describing, and whether or not he is right about copper, he may well be right about the stock market.

So for most readers the question this week has little to do with buying copper. The question is whether the paper market is telling you a bear market has started.

data.title: AARP Is Introducing A New Annuity Program — What Retirees Should Know Before Buying
data.description:
The AARP Annuity Program from Jackson launched November 16, 2026, offering four retirement annuity products to eligible members in 10 states. PattyPhoto/Shutterstock

SUMMARY:

  • AARP members have four new annuity options. Jackson launched the program November 16, 2026, with products offering fixed interest, index-linked growth, and lifetime income.

  • Availability is limited for now. The program launched in 10 states, with broader availability targeted for the first half of 2027.

  • Your money may not be easy to access. Certain contracts include withdrawal charges, interest adjustments, or other restrictions that could make early withdrawals expensive.

  • AARP isn't the insurance provider. Jackson issues the contracts and pays AARP for use of its name, so retirees should compare the products independently before buying.

A familiar name can make a financial product feel safer, especially when that name is AARP. But before moving $50,000 or $100,000 of retirement savings into a new annuity, it’s worth understanding exactly what you’re buying.

On November 16, 2026, Jackson National Life Insurance Company launched the AARP Annuity Program from Jackson, giving eligible members access to four retirement products designed for different financial needs. Some offer guaranteed interest, others promise lifetime income, and two provide opportunities for growth linked to a stock market index.

That sounds appealing if you’re worried about outliving your savings or losing money in the market. Still, annuities come with rules that can be difficult to understand, particularly when it comes to withdrawals, taxes, and guarantees.

Here’s what retirees should know before signing anything.

The New AARP Program Is Already Available in 10 States

This isn’t a future benefit that members have to wait years to use. The November 16 launch announcement from Jackson confirms that eligible AARP members can now access the program in Arizona, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Louisiana, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and South Dakota. Jackson hopes to expand availability nationally during the first half of 2027, although that timeline could change.

The products are being offered directly to consumers, including retirees who don’t currently work with a financial adviser. If you live outside the initial states, you’ll need to wait until the program becomes available where you live.

Four Products, Four Very Different Approaches to Retirement

Not every annuity does the same thing, and that’s particularly important with this program. Interest Advantage offers a guaranteed interest rate over three or five years, while Growth Advantage uses a five- or seven-year fixed indexed annuity structure tied to the performance of the S&P 500. Income Advantage combines index-linked interest opportunities with a rider providing guaranteed lifetime income, even if the contract value eventually reaches zero.

Lifetime Advantage takes a different approach by converting a lump-sum payment into an income stream designed to last for life. The right choice, if any, depends on whether your priority is preserving savings, earning interest, or receiving predictable retirement income.

A Guaranteed Interest Rate Isn’t the Same as a Bank CD

Interest Advantage might catch the attention of retirees who already keep money in certificates of deposit. Both products can provide a stated interest rate for a defined period, but there’s a major difference in how they’re protected. Bank CDs held at FDIC-insured institutions generally qualify for federal deposit insurance within applicable limits, while annuities are insurance contracts without that protection.

Jackson’s Interest Advantage contract may also impose withdrawal charges or interest adjustments if you need your money before the agreed term ends. Before moving savings out of a CD, compare the interest rate, withdrawal restrictions, tax treatment, and the financial strength of the insurance company.

Stock Market Growth Doesn’t Mean Stock Market Returns

Two of Jackson’s new products offer opportunities to earn interest based on the S&P 500, which may sound like investing in an index fund without the usual market risk. That’s not quite how fixed indexed annuities work. Your money isn’t directly invested in the stocks making up the index, and contractual formulas determine how much interest gets credited to your account.

Caps, participation rates, spreads, or other provisions may limit your earnings, meaning a strong year for the stock market doesn’t guarantee an equally strong return on your annuity. Ask Jackson for a written illustration showing how the product performs under different market conditions, including years when the index declines.

The possibility of receiving money every month for the rest of your life is one of the biggest reasons retirees consider annuities. Jackson’s Lifetime Advantage product offers that type of arrangement in exchange for a single premium payment, with income determined by factors such as your age, contribution, current rates, and payment options.

But turning a large portion of your savings into guaranteed income can mean giving up access to the original lump sum. That matters if you later need money for assisted living, medical expenses, major home repairs, or helping a family member. Before purchasing, determine how much accessible savings you’ll have left after funding the annuity and what happens to payments if you die earlier than expected.

Early Withdrawals Could Cost More Than You Expect

A retiree who feels financially comfortable today might face a very different situation three years from now. Jackson’s product disclosures identify withdrawal charges and possible market value adjustments that can affect the amount available when certain contracts are surrendered or money is withdrawn early. Depending on the contract and timing, the cash withdrawal value could even fall below the original amount invested.

That’s an important distinction because principal protection against certain market losses doesn’t necessarily mean you can withdraw every dollar whenever you want. Request the full surrender-charge schedule and ask what would happen if you needed $20,000 unexpectedly during the first few years.

Who Actually Guarantees Your Money?

The word “guaranteed” carries considerable weight when you’re trying to protect savings that took decades to accumulate. However, the guarantees attached to Jackson’s annuities depend on the claims-paying ability of Jackson National Life Insurance Company. They aren’t backed by the FDIC or guaranteed by the federal government.

State insurance guaranty associations may provide limited protection if an insurer becomes insolvent, but those protections vary and shouldn’t be treated as a substitute for evaluating the company. Before purchasing, review Jackson’s financial strength ratings and understand exactly which contract benefits are guaranteed.

AARP’s Name Comes With an Important Disclosure

Seeing AARP attached to a financial product may create an impression that the organization is personally recommending it. The relationship is more specific than that. Under the program’s official disclosures, Jackson pays AARP a royalty for using its intellectual property, while an AARP affiliate receives compensation for managing the group marketing program. Those payments aren’t tied to individual annuity sales, and AARP and its affiliates aren’t acting as the insurer, insurance agent, or seller.

In fact, the disclosures state that AARP doesn’t recommend or endorse the products, making independent comparison especially important before committing retirement savings.

No Sales Commission Doesn’t Mean No Financial Tradeoffs

Jackson describes the four products as non-commissionable, which may appeal to consumers concerned about how annuities are sold. However, the absence of a traditional sales commission doesn’t mean the contracts have no costs or limitations. Insurers still account for expenses and financial risks when setting interest rates, crediting formulas, and income benefits.

A product may have no separate upfront commission while still limiting growth opportunities or charging for certain withdrawals. Focus on what you’ll receive, what you could give up, and how the contract compares with similar products from other insurers.

Taxes Could Change the Financial Picture

Annuities can offer tax-deferred growth, but that doesn’t mean the money you eventually receive will be tax-free. Earnings withdrawn from nonqualified annuities are generally taxed as ordinary income, while annuities held inside retirement accounts follow the tax rules applicable to those accounts.

Purchasing an annuity within a traditional IRA generally doesn’t provide additional tax deferral because the IRA already has that benefit. Large taxable withdrawals may also increase income enough to affect Medicare premiums through income-related monthly adjustments. Before buying, consider how annuity payments would fit alongside Social Security, pensions, required minimum distributions, and other retirement income.

Compare the Annuity With What You Already Have

A new retirement product doesn’t automatically fill a gap in your financial plan. Someone who already receives enough Social Security and pension income to cover essential expenses may not need another guaranteed income stream. Another retiree who depends heavily on investment withdrawals might value predictable payments, even if that means sacrificing some flexibility. CDs, Treasury securities, other insurers’ annuities, and diversified investments all deserve consideration based on the purpose the money needs to serve.

A financial professional who isn’t compensated for selling the product can help evaluate the trade-offs without making the AARP branding the deciding factor.

Before purchasing, ask how long your money will be restricted, what withdrawals are permitted without charges, and whether interest-crediting terms can change. Find out what happens to the contract if you die, whether a spouse can continue receiving payments, and how inflation might affect the purchasing power of fixed income. Request a complete illustration and compare it with at least one similar product from another insurer. If you can’t explain the basic costs, guarantees, and restrictions in your own words, there’s no reason to rush into a purchase.

A Familiar Name Shouldn’t Replace Careful Financial Planning

The AARP Annuity Program from Jackson gives members additional ways to pursue predictable income and protection from certain market losses. For some retirees, those features may address legitimate concerns about retirement security. Others may find that withdrawal restrictions, limited growth potential, or the loss of access to a lump sum outweigh the benefits. What matters most isn’t the organization whose name appears on the marketing materials, but whether the contract supports your actual financial needs.

Would you consider purchasing an annuity through an AARP-branded program, or would you prefer to keep your retirement savings in more flexible accounts?

data.title: Chart Of The Week: America’s Stunning AI Advantage
data.description:
China has found ways to compete with America’s leading AI companies at a fraction of the cost.

And the troubling scandal involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang raised new concerns about America’s ability to keep its most advanced AI technology out of China’s hands.

But despite these challenges, there’s some very encouraging news about America’s position in the global AI race.

And this week’s chart puts that advantage into perspective.

Because new research reveals that America’s lead in one of the most important areas of artificial intelligence is much bigger than most people realize.

And our lead is actually growing.

America’s AI Hardware Advantage

Our chart this week comes from Epoch AI, an organization that studies the development of artificial intelligence.

Its researchers examined customs records and semiconductor production data to estimate where the world’s AI computing hardware has been going since 2022.

You can see the results here:

Between 2022 and June 2026, the United States accounted for approximately 72% of the world’s newly supplied AI computing power.

China accounted for less than 10%.

That’s an advantage of more than 7 to 1.

As I’ve explained in my recent articles about Nvidia (NVDA), these chips are essential for training and running advanced AI models. That’s why Washington has spent years trying to restrict China’s access to America’s most advanced processors.

But according to Epoch AI’s findings, America’s lead appears to be growing.

The United States received roughly 60% to 63% of the world’s new AI computing power annually between 2022 and 2024. That share climbed to approximately 72% in 2025, and during the first six months of 2026, it reached an astonishing 78%.

In other words, even as China has been pouring billions of dollars into developing its own AI industry, America has been gaining an even larger share of the world’s new computing capacity.

That’s because not all AI chips are created equal.

China has been working hard to develop domestic alternatives to Nvidia’s advanced processors. And as I mentioned yesterday, companies like Huawei have made progress building chips that can train and run AI models.

But these processors generally can’t match the computing performance of the most advanced chips available to American technology companies.

That difference shows up clearly in Epoch AI’s research.

China received an estimated 18% of the world’s AI chips by number during the period studied. But those chips represented less than 10% of the total computing power.

That’s a huge distinction when you consider the news that dropped last week.

Because having a million older or less powerful processors isn’t nearly the same as having a million of Nvidia’s most advanced GPUs.

Of course, China isn’t standing still.

As I’ve explained before, companies like DeepSeek have demonstrated that they can build competitive AI systems while using fewer resources than their American rivals.

China has other advantages too, including enormous electricity generation capacity and a manufacturing industry capable of producing advanced technology at scale.

Those strengths shouldn’t be underestimated.

But neither should America’s lead in the hardware that powers today’s most advanced AI systems.

Here’s My Take

China is making impressive progress in AI, and they have no intention of slowing down.

But this week’s chart shows just how big America’s hardware advantage remains.

We have the world’s leading AI chip designers, some of its most advanced AI models and the computing power to keep pushing the technology forward.

That doesn’t guarantee America will win the AI race.

But it puts us in an excellent position to stay ahead.

data.title: Nvidia Doubles Revenue To $115.8 Billion. Wall Street Still Finds Something To Complain About
data.description:
Nvidia (NVDA) just delivered the kind of earnings report most corporate executives would frame and hang above their desks.

Revenue doubled. Profits surged. Demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure remained extraordinary. Management forecast another massive quarter.

Wall Street responded by selling the stock.

Nvidia shares declined nearly 3% on November 18, despite the company reporting $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, an increase of 103% from the previous year.

Apparently, doubling your business is no longer sufficient. Investors would also appreciate perfect margins, unlimited growth, regulatory certainty and a permanent chief executive.

Preferably by Friday.

Behind the sarcasm sits a serious financial question. Has Nvidia become a company whose operating performance is exceptional but whose stock price demands something even better?

Nvidia Earnings: The Numbers Are Difficult to Ignore

Nvidia reported fiscal third-quarter 2027 revenue of $115.8 billion for the period ending October 25, 2026.

That represented 103% annual growth and a 20% increase from the preceding quarter.

Data Center revenue reached $107.6 billion, up 110% from a year earlier.

GAAP net income climbed to $65.3 billion from $31.9 billion.

Diluted earnings per share increased to $2.70 from $1.30.

The company’s GAAP gross margin reached 74.8%.

These are extraordinary numbers for a business operating at Nvidia’s scale.

The company generated approximately $86.7 billion in quarterly gross profit. That means Nvidia retained nearly 75 cents of gross profit for every dollar of revenue before operating expenses.

For perspective, many established industrial businesses would consider a fraction of that margin attractive.

Nvidia is producing it while selling hardware into one of the most capital-intensive technology expansions in history.

Wall Street’s Favorite Problem: Expectations

Nvidia’s financial results were strong. Its stock performance tells a different story.

Reuters reported that shares finished November 18 approximately 36% below their October 6 record closing high.

That decline reflects more than a debate about chip demand.

Investors are weighing leadership uncertainty, regulatory exposure, future margins and the sustainability of enormous AI infrastructure budgets.

Nvidia’s report marked its 17th consecutive quarterly revenue beat, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters.

Think about that.

Seventeen consecutive quarters of exceeding expectations, and investors are still asking whether the next quarter will be good enough.

The market is forward-looking. Shareholders do not pay for yesterday’s profits. They pay for the earnings they expect tomorrow.

When those expectations become enormous, even outstanding financial performance can struggle to support the valuation.

Nvidia Forecasts $130 Billion Quarter

Management expects approximately $130 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, plus or minus 3%.

That forecast includes an additional reporting week.

The company also expects gross margins between 71% and 72%, below the latest quarter’s roughly 75%.

That projected decline deserves attention.

Higher supply costs can reduce profitability even while revenue continues growing.

If Nvidia generates $130 billion in quarterly sales at a 71% gross margin, gross profit would reach approximately $92.3 billion.

That would exceed the latest quarter’s gross profit in absolute dollars despite a lower margin.

This illustrates why investors need to examine both revenue growth and profitability.

A declining margin is not automatically evidence of a deteriorating business.

But persistent margin compression could become significant if customers gain bargaining power or manufacturing costs increase.

The Leadership Question Nobody Can Ignore

Nvidia is also navigating a major management transition.

Following Jensen Huang’s resignation, Colette Kress is serving as interim chief executive while the board searches for permanent leadership.

Huang’s departure introduces uncertainty at a company closely associated with his technical vision, strategic relationships and industry influence.

Reuters reported that the board rejected his offer to return and engaged an executive search firm.

For investors, the issue extends beyond personality.

Nvidia must maintain product development schedules, customer relationships and capital allocation discipline while changing leadership.

The company’s financial results demonstrate operational strength. They do not eliminate the risks associated with a management transition.

That distinction helps explain why impressive earnings have not automatically restored investor confidence.

AI Infrastructure Is Still Growing

The most important number in Nvidia’s report might be its $107.6 billion in Data Center revenue.

That figure demonstrates the scale of spending on artificial intelligence computing infrastructure.

Cloud providers and AI developers continue investing in increasingly powerful systems.

Nvidia has begun shipping its Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, expanding its next-generation computing architecture.

But powerful chips represent only one part of the investment cycle.

Data centers require electricity, cooling, networking equipment, power distribution and physical facilities.

Companies such as Vertiv (VRT), Eaton (ETN) and GE Vernova (GEV) participate in different parts of that infrastructure market.

Their opportunities depend on continued investment, successful project execution and attractive pricing.

The AI expansion could support demand across multiple industries.

Investors still need to distinguish between companies benefiting from industry growth and stocks already priced for extraordinary results.

China Remains a Regulatory Complication

Nvidia’s fourth-quarter forecast assumes no Data Center computing revenue from China.

Management cited the existing export-control environment while expressing confidence that demand elsewhere could support growth.

This creates an unusual situation.

Nvidia faces substantial global demand but cannot necessarily sell every product into every market.

Export restrictions can affect revenue opportunities, customer relationships and supply-chain decisions.

They also make long-term forecasting more complicated.

Investors must separate underlying demand from the company’s legal ability to fulfill orders.

Strong customer interest does not guarantee completed sales.

What Investors Should Watch Next

The next several quarters will test three important assumptions.

First, can Nvidia sustain exceptional revenue growth as its business becomes larger?

data.title: Everybody’s In On Anthropic Except Apple

I mean, even Zoom was sharp enough to get into this one.

data.title: Would The Fed Hike Interest Rates In A Month Where The CPI Is Negative?
data.description:
We may find out in December.

The Fed meets on December 9, 2026.

It is a near certainty the Fed hikes interest rates. Call it 99+ percent.

Despite a lot of chatter about a 50 basis point hike, that’s not going to happen no matter how bad the PCE report is on November 26.

Question of the Day

Negative CPI Reading Quite Possible

Energy prices will decline.

And if there is very tame Owners’ Equivalent Rent (OER) it can easily happen.

Shelter is over 35 percent of the CPI with OER nearly 26 percent. Energy was 7.65 percent of the CPI in October.

If shelter comes in flat, and energy is down big, we are going to see a negative CPI reading the day after the Fed hikes.

Energy Q&A With Grok

Mish: What is the projection for the energy component of the CPI report for November?

Grok: Projections for the energy component of the November 2026 CPI (due for release December 10, 2026) point to a significant decline, on the order of roughly −2.5% month-over-month. globalmacrolens.com

The most detailed publicly available nowcast comes from GlobalMacroLens (updated as of November 19, 2026). It estimates the energy component at −2.53% m/m (weight ~7.2%), contributing about −0.184 percentage points to headline CPI.

This is derived from weekly EIA fuel prices (among other free public data) to bridge the energy leaves of the CPI basket. The same nowcast puts headline CPI at about +0.04% m/m (3.9% y/y) and core at +0.25% m/m (2.9% y/y). globalmacrolens.com

Prediction markets (e.g., Kalshi) price headline around −0.1% m/m / 3.7% y/y.

GlobalMacroLens Baseline

What Would It Take to Go Negative?

You only need roughly another −0.05 pp of contribution to reach something like −0.01% (or a bit more for a clearer negative print).

  • Energy alone: An extra ~0.7 percentage-point decline (i.e., energy around −3.2% to −3.5% m/m instead of −2.5%) would do it, all else equal. That is plausible if the late-month gasoline drop is a bit steeper than the weekly EIA data already embedded in the nowcast.

  • Shelter help: Because of its high weight, a 0.1 pp slower shelter reading (e.g., +0.15–0.20% instead of the recent ~0.3% pace) adds roughly another −0.035 pp of drag.

  • Combination (the most realistic path): Energy at roughly −3.0% m/m + shelter closer to +0.15–0.20% (or even just a bit softer than the +0.29% core-services assumption) easily clears the zero line. Food or core-goods softness would help further but is not required.

Grok Comment: This lines up with market pricing (Kalshi median around −0.1% m/m) and commentary noting that the sharp gasoline/oil drop is the main swing factor for a soft headline print. Shelter is slower-moving and less likely to surprise dramatically to the downside in a single month, so the energy outcome is the bigger variable.

Genuine Tossup

I give a lot of credence to the betting markets.

So, I am upping my 35 percent chance off the top of my head answer to Michael Lebowitz.

I now think a Fed hike in a month with a negative CPI reading is a genuine tossup, if not slightly odds on.

Note that the BLS rounds to a single digit. Thus -0.049 would get rounded to 0.0.

I calculate to two digits. If the judge is a two digit calculation, I think the odds are 60 percent that the discussed event occurs. Otherwise, flip a coin.

On cruises, CEO Josh D’Amaro said Disney would add ships faster if it could get them built to its standards. That’s a pretty direct answer to a question about whether Disney would need promotions to fill the rooms it’s already added.

Disney is already seeing some of the benefit from its next Avengers movie, and it doesn’t hit theaters until December 18th. After the trailer for Avengers: Doomsday came out this summer and Spider-Man: Brand New Day drew crowds to theaters, August was the biggest month ever for Marvel Studios viewing on Disney+. data.title: Fed Hawks Turn Up Heat As Inflation Fears Grow
data.description:
Federal Reserve Governor Chris Waller didn’t mince words.

“I’m very, very concerned about inflation,” he told CNBC on Wednesday. “It’s kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out. If you really want to get it down, you’ve got to start taking more aggressive actions. You might need to, like, shock people.”

As a first installment on shocking sentiment he said a half-point rate hike at next month’s FOMC meeting is warranted.

Other Fed officials have made similarly hawkish comments this week. St. Louis Fed president Alberto Musalem said that inflation is too high, is becoming broad based and so more policy tightening is needed, advising that “the economy will likely require several interest ​rate increases before the spring of 2027 ​to achieve price stability in a timely manner.”

The Treasury market has been pricing in higher odds for a series of rate hikes for months. The policy-sensitive 2-year yield (widely viewed as a proxy for near-term Fed rate expectations) has eased in recent days, but the upward trend is still strong, closing at 4.81% on Wednesday. That’s well above the Fed’s current 3.75%-4.0% target rate, a spread that indicates strong market confidence that hikes are likely.

A simple model using unemployment and the one-year change for consumer prices suggests that current Fed policy is roughly neutral. But with inflation continuing to run above the 2% target, and recent updates suggesting pricing pressure is spreading, the central bank is under growing pressure to continue tightening. Neutral, in other words, is no longer sufficient and the ¼-point hike in September – the first in three years — is increasingly viewed as the start of an extended round of tightening.

Fed funds futures are pricing in a 90% probability of a ¼-point hike at the upcoming Dec. 9 FOMC meeting. A 70% probability is the current estimate for a follow-up hike in January.

Robust economic data is a factor that’s also tilting expectations toward additional rate hikes. One input is the low unemployment rate, which slipped to 4.1% in October, which is historically low and down from 4.5% a year ago. The four-week average of jobless claims held at 195,250 through Nov. 7, the lowest in decades. Meanwhile, the monthly change in nonfarm payrolls rebounded in October, rising 165,000, close to the strongest gain this year. Notably, the one-year change is payrolls has been strengthening for months, rising 0.6% from the year-ago level, marking the fastest increase since April 2025.

Headline economic activity is also reflecting an ongoing pickup lately. The Atlanta Fed’s Q4 GDP nowcast is 3.2%, close to the 3.4% advance reported for Q3. The acceleration in growth from the first half’s slower pace, in other words, is expected to continue.

Additional rate hikes won’t be cost-free. The housing market, in particular, remains under pressure from elevated mortgage rates and weak sales activity. The National Association of Realtors (NAR) reports that existing-home sales in October fell 5.5% to an annualized pace of 3.75 million, the slowest since August 2010. NAR’s chief economist attributed the weakness largely to high mortgage rates. Pending home sales, a leading indicator of future transactions, fell to a record low in October, with NAR citing elevated mortgage rates and affordability constraints. Pushing rates higher, which will lift financing costs, will put more pressure on an already struggling housing sector.

Yet the inflation calculus is likely to dominate Fed decision-making in the near term. Unless price pressures show more convincing signs of easing, policymakers may conclude that the risk of doing too little still outweighs the risk of doing too much. With overall economic growth remaining resilient and the labor market holding up, the economy appears capable of absorbing additional tightening, increasing the odds that interest rates move higher and remain elevated for longer than investors currently expect.
