data.title: TradingView MCP: When Artificial Intelligence Got Its Hands On The Pine Script Compiler
data.description:
A few years ago, developing a trading strategy began with learning a programming language. Then came large language models, and traders could describe their ideas in plain English. There was, however, considerable distance between receiving a piece of source code and having a working strategy. The AI wrote the program, the trader copied it into Pine Editor, the compiler complained, and the trader went back to the AI. Sometimes this exchange of pleasantries lasted longer than the development of the trading idea itself.

On November 16, 2026, TradingView gave AI agents access to its native Pine Script compiler and strategy backtesting engine through its own MCP server. Against the relentless stream of artificial intelligence announcements, the news could easily go unnoticed. Yet for the algorithmic trading industry, it may prove considerably more significant than the arrival of another language model.

TradingView has reduced the need for a human intermediary between artificial intelligence and the development environment.

A Compiler at the Other End of the Conversation

The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is an open standard that allows AI applications to interact with external software. In TradingView's case, the agent communicates with the same computational infrastructure that powers the platform itself.

The language model can now receive feedback directly from the compiler, including line numbers, error positions and warnings. It can correct a program, validate it again and run it against historical market data.

TradingView has introduced eight tools for working with Pine Script:

  • validate_pine_script — validates source code.

  • run_pine_indicator — calculates indicator values.

  • run_pine_backtest — runs a trading strategy backtest.

  • get_pine_script_source — retrieves accessible source code.

  • get_pine_script_info — retrieves script parameters and output information.

  • search_pine_scripts — searches for scripts.

  • create_pine_script and update_pine_script — create and update scripts within the user's account.

When a program is updated, TradingView preserves its previous versions, while code that fails compilation is not saved to the account. Intermediate experiments can be conducted without saving the source code. Other authors' protected and invite-only publications remain inaccessible.

What is particularly noteworthy is that TradingView has not built a separate development environment for artificial intelligence. Instead, it has opened the existing infrastructure that Pine Script developers have been using for years.

Connecting TradingView to Artificial Intelligence

The official MCP server is available here.

The connection uses Streamable HTTP with OAuth 2.1 authorization. TradingView supports ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, Cursor and other compatible applications. Users simply add the appropriate connector and authorize access through their TradingView account. Detailed instructions are available in the official MCP documentation.

While preparing this article, I connected TradingView to ChatGPT and tried the new integration while developing a strategy based on liquidity sweeps and false breakouts. The purpose was to see how much of the development and testing process could be delegated to the AI agent. The trading idea did not automatically become profitable, but the need to constantly transfer code and test results between applications was considerably reduced. The first noticeable restriction was the number of available requests.

For developers accustomed to working with Pine Editor and Strategy Tester, this way of interacting with the platform may initially feel unfamiliar. After a few iterations, however, it becomes apparent how much time was previously spent on tasks that required neither market knowledge nor any particular programming talent.

Backtesting Is No Longer a Manual Exercise

Throughout the history of financial technology, the cost of computation has repeatedly determined who could afford to employ particular methods of market research. Computing power once reserved for large banks and investment firms gradually found its way onto the retail trader's desk. Now the distance between a trading hypothesis and its computational investigation is shrinking as well.

Through MCP, artificial intelligence can access Strategy Tester statistics: net profit, profit factor, maximum drawdown, total trades, percentage of profitable positions, average profits and losses, and Sharpe and Sortino ratios. The agent can examine individual trades and compare the performance of long and short positions. With an eligible subscription, Deep Backtesting allows research over a specified historical period.

The investigation of a trading system rarely ends with its first successful backtest. It remains necessary to determine how much the results depend on the instrument, timeframe, indicator parameters and prevailing market conditions. Sometimes changing a single number is enough to make a splendid set of statistics disappear.

Until now, such work required considerable involvement from the developer. A sequence of experiments can increasingly be delegated to an AI agent, leaving the human responsible for defining the research question and interpreting the results.

An equally important change concerns the quality of the software itself. One longstanding criticism of language models is their ability to produce entirely nonfunctional programs with disarming confidence. Access to the compiler and execution results makes it possible to uncover many of these mistakes during development. It also becomes easier to establish whether correcting one part of a strategy has inadvertently damaged another.

The quality of AI-assisted software development will improve not only because language models are becoming more capable, but because their mistakes are becoming easier to expose.

There is, of course, another side to this development. Curve-fitting trading strategies to historical data existed long before artificial intelligence. MCP could turn it into an industrial operation. An agent instructed to maximize profitability may discover a magnificent combination of parameters that proves entirely useless outside the period under investigation.

The market is under no obligation to repeat history simply because a computer has learned to study it faster.

Ten Calls Before Breakfast

Beginning November 17, 2026, TradingView applies the following daily MCP usage limits:

The additional AI subscription also carries a limit of 50 requests per minute. Usage limits reflect TradingView’s documentation at publication and may change.

These figures deserve some attention. A single question put to an AI assistant may require several calls to TradingView. Compiling a program, running a backtest, validating a correction and saving a script are separate operations, each consuming part of the overall allowance.

Ten requests may seem perfectly adequate to an occasional chatbot user. A trading system developer could exhaust them before breakfast.

Having removed a human bottleneck from Pine Script development, TradingView has introduced a computational one. The availability of a paid AI subscription also reveals the commercial logic of the arrangement. The company can now sell not only access to analytical tools, but additional computational capacity for artificial intelligence.

In the coming years, the cost of a research iteration may become a factor in its own right when choosing a trading platform.

MetaTrader Is Keeping Pace

TradingView is hardly alone in this endeavor. On July 23, 2026, MetaQuotes introduced MetaTrader 5 Build 6060, with native support for MCP and agentic artificial intelligence. The integration extends across the trading terminal and MetaEditor, allowing AI agents to work with MQL5 source code, compile programs, and test and optimize Expert Advisors. Further details are available in the MetaEditor MCP and AI documentation. Unlike TradingView, MetaTrader's implementation also extends to trading operations. Within four months, two of the largest ecosystems in retail algorithmic trading have given artificial intelligence direct access to development tools previously operated by humans. That is hardly a coincidence.

From Source Code to an Actual Trade

TradingView has drawn a fairly clear distinction between strategy research and trade execution. Its MCP terms of use prohibit using the server for automated trading, trading decisions or connections to trading bots.

For the execution of separately developed and tested strategies, the established mechanism remains trading alerts and webhooks. A Pine Script signal is passed to external software that communicates with a trading platform or broker. This is a separate workflow, not permission to connect TradingView’s MCP server or its alerts to automated trading systems.

As the development of trading algorithms becomes more accessible, demand for execution infrastructure is likely to grow as well. Broker restrictions, position sizing, duplicate signal handling and discrepancies between simulated and actual execution will remain very much a part of the business.

Artificial intelligence considerably simplifies the development of a trading system, but the financial responsibility for its operation still rests with the owner of the trading account.

Storm Clouds Over Alternative Compilers

TradingView's November announcement arrives at a rather inconvenient moment for several young projects born out of Pine Script's limitations. PyneCore and PyneComp offer a route for bringing trading algorithms into Python, while PineForge translates Pine Script v6 into C++ and provides its own backtesting engine, accessible through MCP. PyneCore's developers report compatibility testing across 1,000 published TradingView scripts, while PineForge presents results from nearly 8,000 backtests. These are the projects' own published findings, not independent assessments of their compatibility with the original.

The engineering value of these developments cannot be dismissed. Independent execution, proprietary market datasets and large-scale testing remain attractive propositions, particularly in light of TradingView's daily quotas. Yet as recently as last week, the ability to backtest Pine Script from an AI client without human intervention looked like a substantial competitive advantage. Now the owner of the language itself provides access to the original compiler, historical market data and its native execution environment. Selling independence from TradingView may remain a profitable business. Selling an alternative to its compiler solely for the convenience of AI-assisted development will become considerably harder. Storm clouds are gathering over this young market, and, ironically enough, they have come from TradingView's own cloud infrastructure.

All references and external links are provided solely for readers' convenience and independent research.

data.title: AMD Stock Falls 7% As Hunterbrook Alleges Links To Blacklisted Chinese Firm
data.description:
AMD stock fell 7% on Thursday after Hunterbrook Media, an investigative publication affiliated with short seller Hunterbrook Capital, alleged that the chipmaker's firmware was being used by a blacklisted Chinese company and three businesses linked to it.

The report claimed that IEIT Systems, a Chinese server maker, had incorporated at least six newer versions of AMD's firmware into its products after being placed on the US government's export blacklist.

Hunterbrook also alleged that three other server companies with links to IEIT offered products containing closely matching firmware, raising questions about whether servers designed by the blacklisted company were being sold through other businesses.

The revelations were made in a report called 'AMD has its own China problem'.

Hunterbrook Media disclosed that, at the time of publication, its affiliated investment firm Hunterbrook Capital was short AMD shares and held long positions in a basket of comparable securities.

The report drew parallels with the controversy surrounding Nvidia's (NVDA) sales of advanced chips to Chinese companies and questioned whether AMD could genuinely be considered a safer alternative to its larger rival.

AMD's China exposure comes under scrutiny

The firm has questioned a growing perception that AMD is a less risky way to gain exposure to the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom amid scrutiny of Nvidia's China business.

The firm highlighted that AMD shares gained nearly 45% in the five sessions through November 12, the day Nvidia announced CEO Jensen Huang's resignation in what CNBC reported was a board decision to oust him.

William Blair and Oppenheimer also upgraded AMD during that period, according to Hunterbrook.

However, the publication argued that investors may be underestimating AMD's exposure to the same geopolitical and regulatory risks facing Nvidia.

As of the November 18 close, AMD traded at around 30 times its estimated earnings for the next fiscal year, compared with approximately nine times for Nvidia, based on analyst estimates published by Yahoo Finance.

"The Bear Cave believes investors are trading one cousin’s problems for the other’s," the report said, referring to Jensen Huang's relationship with AMD chief Lisa Su, who is his cousin.

The Bear Cave is an investigative newsletter owned by Hunterbrook Media.

IEIT allegedly used AMD firmware after blacklisting

Hunterbrook said the US Commerce Department placed IEIT on its Entity List in March 2025.

The designation means that exports of items covered by US export controls to the company require a licence, with the department's stated policy being to deny such applications.

Despite the restrictions, IEIT has incorporated at least six newer versions of AMD's firmware into its products since being blacklisted, according to the investigation.

The latest version identified by Hunterbrook appeared in an updated product listing posted on October 19.

The report also identified three companies that sell servers built around AMD chips under their own brands: Maginfra in China, Kaytus in Singapore and Aivres in California.

"Hunterbrook found that the firmware they offer is nearly identical to IEIT’s, suggesting they may be selling servers designed by the blacklisted company. Corporate filings point the same way: IEIT’s 2022 annual report listed Aivres, then called Inspur Systems, as a subsidiary. Kaytus’s own audited accounts name IEIT as its ultimate parent company," it said.

The investigation also highlighted other alleged links between AMD and entities subject to US restrictions.

Hunterbrook said AMD reported $67 million in licensing income in 2025 that the publication traced to two Chinese chip ventures blacklisted in 2019.

It also identified a server from Cancon, an alias of the blacklisted company Suma, in AMD's February 2026 product catalogue.

"In sum: AMD appears no less at risk from China chip restrictions than Nvidia, despite the recent surge of positive coverage," Hunterbrook said.

Potential changes to export rules could add pressure

The report also warned that changes to US export regulations could expose AMD to additional restrictions on its international business.

A suspension of a rule that would extend export restrictions to foreign companies at least 50% owned by blacklisted entities is due to expire on January 10, 2027.

If implemented, the provision could expand restrictions to Kaytus and other foreign companies in which IEIT holds at least a 50% stake, it said.

Separately, a newly released interim final rule, which takes effect on Thursday, will require licences for advanced chips shipped to Singapore and four other countries.

The potential impact on AMD could be significant given its business in the region.

The company recorded $4.28 billion in billings to customers in Singapore during fiscal 2025, accounting for more than 10% of its total sales.

"For AMD, this could mean additional licensing requirements that can delay or block sales," Hunterbrook said.

data.title: Anthropic Vs. OpenAI: Who’s Winning The AI Race?
data.description:
Who’s Ahead in the Race Between Anthropic and OpenAI?

Key Takeaways

  • Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 leads the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 64.6 as of Nov. 17, 2026, ahead of OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra at 62.1.

  • Anthropic (ANT) has held the lead for seven consecutive months since April 2026, its longest stretch in front, after leadership changed hands eight times between September 2024 and April 2026.

  • The two companies released 13 frontier models in 2026 through mid-November, more than the 11 released in 2024 and 2025 combined.

The rivalry between Anthropic and OpenAI has become one of the defining competitions in artificial intelligence. Each new flagship model offers another chance to claim the top spot on AI intelligence benchmarks.

This graphic tracks the highest scores achieved by each company on the Artificial Analysis (AA) Intelligence Index over time. It includes Anthropic’s Opus and Fable models and OpenAI’s leading GPT and o-series models, showing only releases that set a new high for their company.

The index currently combines nine tests covering knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge. AA updated its methodology on Oct. 27, so scores before and after that date are not directly comparable.

Anthropic Has Had the Smartest AI Models Since April 2026

For much of the AI race, neither Anthropic nor OpenAI could hold onto the top spot for long. Between May 2025 and April 2026 alone, leadership changed seven times, with some advantages lasting only weeks.

That pattern changed when Anthropic’s Opus 4.7 overtook OpenAI in April 2026. Despite a steady stream of new releases from both companies, Anthropic has remained ahead on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index ever since.

The table below lists every model on the chart in order of release, along with its score on each version of the index:

Scores for models released before Opus 4.8 (May 2026) are Artificial Analysis estimates. Version 5.0.1 scores are shown for models plotted after the Oct. 27 methodology change.

Some victories in the AI race have been remarkably short-lived. Anthropic’s Opus 4.5 held the lead for just 17 days before OpenAI’s GPT-5.2 overtook it in December 2025.

The longer-term picture is more balanced than the current streak suggests. Since March 2024, Anthropic has spent 529 days in front, compared with 459 days for OpenAI. That makes its current run especially significant in a competition where leadership has historically been difficult to maintain.

Anthropic’s lead also survived AA’s Oct. 27 update, which added two tests, upgraded three, and removed three.

However, different benchmarks can produce different winners. On Epoch AI’s Capabilities Index, OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra leads with a score of 174.2, narrowly ahead of Fable 5.2 at 173.5. The difference falls within both models’ margins of error.

Frontier AI Model Releases Have Doubled in Pace This Year

The competition has also accelerated. In 2025, Anthropic and OpenAI released a new frontier model roughly every 52 days. In 2026, that interval has shortened to about 25 days, with 13 releases through mid-November.

Anthropic has driven much of that pace, accounting for eight of the 13 releases this year. OpenAI has often responded within days. GPT-6 Astra arrived two days after Fable 5.1 and scored 0.7 points lower. In November, GPT-6.2 Astra followed Fable 5.2 by eight days and finished 2.4 points behind.

But benchmark leadership is only one measure of success. OpenAI also faces growing competition in the broader AI chatbot market, where user adoption tells a different story.

ChatGPT accounted for 88% of global AI chatbot website traffic at the end of 2024, but its share fell to 56% by September 2026 as Anthropic’s Claude and Google (GOOGL) Gemini gained ground.

data.title: Why The Biggest IPO Ever Matters For Gold Investors
data.description:
On October 29, I wrote that when gold falls on supportive news, the sellers are in control. Gold is about $300 lower now.

At the moment of writing these words, December gold futures trade near $3,720, after moving down to $3,694.50 overnight, their lowest level since September 2, 2025. Silver futures trade near $45, and the GDXJ, the ETF for junior mining stocks, closed at $90.07 on Wednesday, its lowest close since November 2025. Meanwhile, the stock futures are higher ahead of the debut of Anthropic, whose IPO is the biggest on record.

The rule about the sellers works in the stock market too, and Wednesday showed it. 

Stocks Ignored the Best News of the Week

On October 29, when December gold futures traded near $4,033, I wrote: "When gold falls on a day that should support it, the sellers are in control. In my view, this is bearish information." Since then, gold has declined by about 8 percent.

On Wednesday, stocks had every reason to rally. Nvidia's (NVDA) revenue rose 103 percent from a year earlier and beat expectations; Target (TGT) and Lowe's (LOW) beat expectations as well, oil fell, and the 10-year Treasury yield slipped to 5.06 percent. The S&P 500 fell anyway. It lost 0.23 percent, to 7,323.63, its fifth decline in a row and its lowest close since July 29. The sellers are in control of stocks too, and this matters for the stock market's relationship with gold, because the miners are stocks as well.

It's also notable that the S&P 500 isn't soaring from its lows the way it did before. In late July, it gained 1.66 percent on the day after its July 29 close. In early November, it soared on the third day: after the lows of November 5 and 6, it gained 2.35 percent on November 9. This morning, the S&P 500 futures are up about 1.2 percent, which isn't much after five declines in a row.

Tech stocks are holding up better. On Wednesday, the Nasdaq 100 gained 0.42 percent, while the S&P 500 lost 0.23 percent, and this morning, the Nasdaq 100 futures are up about 2 percent. In my view, this could be based on the hype around Anthropic's (ANT) IPO, and it could be overstated.

That hype deserves a closer look, because hyped listings have a track record. 

What Hyped Listings Have Told Us About Tops

On Wednesday evening, Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, above the $70-78 range, at a valuation of about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis. Its shares start trading on Nasdaq today under the ticker ANT.

SpaceX (SPCX) is the freshest example of what came next in such cases. It priced its IPO at $135 on June 11 and reached $225.64 on June 16, its third day of trading. That was the top. By mid-July, SpaceX traded below its IPO price, and on Wednesday, it closed at $143.50, about 36 percent below the June high.

Silver did the same in 2006, when the first big silver ETF was launched. The iShares Silver Trust (SLV) started trading on April 28, 2006. Silver kept rallying for less than two weeks, and the gain was less than 20 percent. It topped on May 11, and within about a month, it fell about 35 percent.

There are more examples. Palm's (PALMV) IPO in March 2000 came 6 trading days before the Nasdaq's record close at the peak of the dot-com bubble, and the index then lost 78 percent. Rivian's (RIVN) IPO in November 2021 came 7 trading days before the Nasdaq's record close of that cycle.

Not every hyped listing marks the top of the entire market. After SpaceX's IPO, the Nasdaq Composite kept rising until its October 6 record. Anthropic, though, is listing into a market that's already falling: the Nasdaq 100 closed on Wednesday about 13 percent below its October 6 record, and Nvidia closed at its lowest level since June 2025 despite beating expectations. 

Why Hyped Listings Tend to Come Near Tops

There are three reasons. The first is new supply. Anthropic's IPO and private placement brought $107.3 billion of new shares to the market, five months after SpaceX's $75 billion IPO set the previous record, and to buy the new shares, many investors sell other stocks. The second is that insiders choose when to sell. Companies and their early investors go public when buyers are willing to pay the most, which is why IPOs cluster after strong markets. The third is that nobody might be left to buy. Those who want the hyped stock buy it in the first days, and after that, the sellers take over.

In my view, this IPO might be happening at the peak of the AI hype or right after it peaked, and it could be the final moment when the enthusiasm peaks. Anthropic's valuation of about $1.5 trillion is up from $965 billion in its private funding round in May. It might not be realistic, and investors might realize that and sell the stock, even though AI technology is revolutionary.

If that happens, the miners are likely to feel it first. 

Why the Miners Fall Harder

When stocks decline, the mining stocks tend to fall more than gold, because investors sell them as stocks first and as gold proxies second. On Wednesday, the GDXJ fell 6.02 percent, almost twice as much as gold, on a day when the S&P 500 lost only 0.23 percent.

On October 26, after gold slipped below $4,000, I wrote: "Until the miners start rising on gold's down days, or at least falling less than gold, I think the decline in the sector has further to go." Since then, the GDXJ has lost about 9 percent, and gold about 7 percent. The miners are still falling more than gold, and on Wednesday, the GDXJ broke down to new 2026 lows, also in terms of the closing prices.

Gold itself reached an important level overnight. 

Gold Reaches Its Declining Support Line

On September 10, when gold traded near $4,400, I wrote that a daily close below the neckline of gold's head-and-shoulders top, then near $4,320, "would complete the formation with its target below $4,000." Since then, gold has declined by about 15 percent.

Now, gold has moved down to its declining support line, and such gold support levels often slow a decline, so a pause is possible here, also in silver and the mining stocks.

One of my Gold Trading Alerts subscribers asked in the comments whether I expect any rally attempts before gold reaches about $3,500. It's a good question, and I'm happy to answer it here as well. In short, a pause is possible here, but I don't expect a meaningful rally before the next leg lower. In April 2013, no consolidation followed the breakdown: gold crashed 10.8 percent to its April 16 low, and the 12.6 percent correction came only after that. In my view, a sizable gold price correction is more likely to start from lower prices than from current prices. On a side note, I just updated my final downside target for gold - $3,500 is just the first one.

Before I sum up, there's one more thing worth celebrating today. 

Happy International Men's Day

Today, November 19, is International Men's Day. Dr. Jerome Teelucksingh from Trinidad and Tobago first celebrated it in 1999, and it's now marked in more than 80 countries. The day celebrates the positive value that men bring to the world, their families and their communities, and this year's theme is "The Future Is Everyone."

To all the men reading this: Happy International Men's Day! I wish you good health, strength and plenty of time with the people who matter most to you. If there's a check-up that you've been postponing, today is a good day to book it. You are important. And if that doesn’t convince you, think of your body as a business asset – you don’t want it to depreciate too fast… And to all the women reading this: thank you for celebrating with us. 

Where This Leaves Us

The stock market ignored the best news of the week, and today, the biggest IPO on record debuts into a market that's already falling. Hyped listings have often come near tops, and when stocks decline, the miners tend to fall harder than gold. Gold reached its declining support line, so a pause is possible here, but in my view, gold is likely to decline to at least $3,500. In today's Gold Trading Alert, I also updated my long-term gold chart and my view on where this decline is most likely to end, and I described my plan for the next two trades.

When the last buyers are in, the hype ends, and the miners are usually the first to feel it.

data.title: XEQT Vs GEQT: Which All-In-One ETF Fits Your Retirement?
data.description:
XEQT holds about ten times as many companies as GEQT. GEQT puts 64% of its money in two sectors. And its largest position, Nvidia (NVDA), weighs almost twice as much as it does in XEQT.

Both are all-in-one ETFs. Both are 100% stocks. They are not the same bet.

Here is my take before we start. One is a broad market investment. The other is a big bet on tech and financials, even though it is built around your values.

Here is the full comparison on video if you would rather watch it than read it.

What Are XEQT and GEQT?

Two all-in-one equity ETFs. XEQT buys the world, with 8,000 to 9,000 stocks. GEQT is an ESG-screened version with about 800 stocks and no emerging markets.

The idea is the same for both. You buy one ETF, it holds a basket of country ETFs, and it rebalances automatically.

XEQT touches Canada, the US, international and emerging markets. You are everywhere. Almost too much everywhere, because you reach up to 9,000 companies.

GEQT has a similar structure, with one ETF per region. The most important difference is that it is ESG screened: environmental, social and good governance. It excludes fossil fuels, among other things.

One note on that. Read the rules and look at the companies. Whether a stock qualifies as ESG is debatable and depends on your point of view and values.

XEQT vs GEQT: two all-in-one ETFs, two strategies

How Do XEQT and GEQT Compare Side by Side?

Fees and yield are close. Size is not. XEQT has $23.6 billion in net assets and GEQT about $311 million.

Fees: XEQT charges a management fee of 0.17%, reduced in late 2025, and GEQT 0.22%. With the underlying ETFs included, the MER is 0.19% and 0.25%. On $100,000, that is $190 against $250 a year, a $60 gap. Nothing to write home about.

Trailing yield: 1.61% for XEQT and 1.16% for GEQT. Both are low-yield, high-growth products. You will not make a difference here either.

Underlying companies: this is where they split. XEQT holds between 8,000 and 9,000 stocks. GEQT holds about 800.

Net assets: $23.6 billion for XEQT, a popular ETF. About $311 million for GEQT. Not the same ballpark.

Inception: August 2019 for XEQT, September 2020 for GEQT. That gives a little over five years to compare returns. Useful, but not a long track record.

XEQT vs GEQT fees, yield and size, BlackRock data as of November 3, 2026

Where Do They Invest?

Mostly in North America. About 70% for XEQT and 77% for GEQT.

Both hold between 40% and 45% in US stocks. Canada is 25% in XEQT and 31% in GEQT. International markets take 23% of GEQT, with no exposure to emerging markets. XEQT holds more international and adds emerging markets.

So with either one, you are basically investing in North America.

XEQT vs GEQT geographic allocation

How Concentrated Is GEQT?

Very. Technology and financials each take 32% of GEQT, for 64% of the portfolio. In XEQT, those two sectors add up to 44%.

The sectors were the biggest surprise. GEQT has 0% in energy, as you would expect. Then technology at 32% and financials at 32%.

Technology and financials are doing well right now. That’s great. I am still not sure you want two-thirds of your portfolio in two sectors.

At DSR, we flag any sector above 20%. XEQT sits right around that line with technology at 22% and financials at 21%. After that, it spreads out: industrials at 11%, healthcare at 7.7%, energy at 7.5%, and so on.

For GEQT, it is really those two sectors. Add industrials at 8.6% and healthcare at 6%, and you have the bulk of the portfolio. Both ETFs hold very little in communication services, consumer staples, utilities and real estate.

XEQT vs GEQT sector allocation

That 20-point gap matters if you are retired. A portfolio this concentrated can swing very fast.

What Do the Top Holdings Show?

GEQT leans on Nvidia and the Canadian banks. Its top 25 positions make up 39% of the ETF, against 28% for XEQT.

Both like Nvidia. It is about 3% of XEQT and 5.7% of GEQT.

In XEQT, the weights drop fast. Apple is near 3%, Microsoft at 2.4%, Royal Bank at 2%, then Amazon at 1.5%, and the 10th largest position, Bank of Montreal, sits at 0.85%.

GEQT looks completely different. TD Bank at 3.3%, Royal Bank at 3%, Broadcom and Shopify near 3% each, Bank of Montreal and Scotiabank near 2% each. Then Micron at 1.8%, CIBC at 1.74% and AMD at 1.49%. The theme is easy to see: financials and technology.

XEQT vs GEQT top 10 holdings

Three things stand out with GEQT. The big Nvidia weight. Zero Apple, Microsoft, Amazon or Alphabet. And no Meta or Tesla either, while XEQT holds all of them.

You can debate whether Apple or Microsoft are less ESG than Nvidia. I don’t have an opinion on that. You can ask yourself if it is worth it.

Even with 800 companies, GEQT’s top 25 is close to 40% of your money.

Which One Performed Better?

About the same so far. GEQT is slightly ahead since inception. In 2022, though, XEQT fell 11% and GEQT fell 15.7%.

2022 was a bad year for the stock market, and GEQT took the bigger hit. With 800 stocks, you might think it is well diversified. It isn’t diversified enough.

XEQT vs GEQT calendar year total returns since 2022

The big question is whether ESG beat the regular market, or whether GEQT simply holds more chip and semiconductor stocks. That is what has been driving the stock market lately, up and down.

Can These ETFs Pay for Your Retirement?

Not through the yield. Both pay well under 2%. The money comes from total return, and you sell units to create your income.

I covered this a few weeks ago on a Retirement Friday episode of The Moose on the Loose. Selling units works, and it can generate more income than focusing on income ETFs. The numbers prove it, even through a prolonged bear market like 2008.

Yearly distributions on $100,000 with XEQT and GEQT

In December, I will show Retirement Loop members step by step how selling units to generate income works, and why it holds up.

What Are the Risks?

Four of them. Both are 100% stocks. GEQT is concentrated. GEQT is small, which can widen the bid and ask spread. And both carry currency risk.

100% stocks. Right now it feels like unicorns and rainbows, with double digit returns every year. There is risk there, especially if you are retired. On my side, I will be 100% invested in stocks for the rest of my life. That’s just me. It isn’t necessarily you.

Concentration. 64% in two sectors is a bit too much for my taste. Again, that’s just me.

Liquidity. Check the bid and ask spread on any ETF. XEQT has $23.6 billion in assets, GEQT about $300 million. A smaller ETF can show a bigger spread, which matters for limit orders, and even more if you sell in a panic (which you should not do, but it happens).

Currency. Both trade in Canadian dollars. You still carry foreign currency risk through the US dollar, the euro and Asian currencies. Keep that in mind as you walk into retirement.

XEQT vs GEQT risks to watch

XEQT or GEQT: Which One Is Best for You?

It depends on the bet you want. XEQT buys the broad market. GEQT is a big bet on tech and financials built on an ESG screen.

Ask yourself three questions before you pick either one.

  • Do you want the broad market or a screened version of it? GEQT is the ESG version. With XEQT, you buy the world.

  • Are you comfortable with the concentration? If you like GEQT, you could pair it with something else to lower the exposure to tech and financials.

  • What is your investment objective? Are you comfortable managing a portfolio built on total return, and generating your own income in retirement? If yes, both are great products. If not, you might want to add fixed income, more dividend-paying stocks or another strategy.

The key is always the same. Find a strategy you understand, one you are comfortable with, and one you will stick to when your portfolio is down 10%. That is how you live a happy retirement.

data.title: Bigger Rug, Bigger Rug Pull
data.description:
Last Friday, we described that day’s activity as a “rug pull.”  On that day, we saw stocks rise in the pre-market and on the open, then sink quickly afterwards.  Today, we’re seeing something similar, though after a much bigger early rally.  Traders were clearly enthusiastic about the prospects for the much-awaited IPO[i] (it has still not opened as I type this), but that stock’s coattails were not long enough to drag the whole market along with it this morning.

The charts below show the dramatic moves in both ES (E-Mini S&P 500) and NQ (Nasdaq 100 E-Mini) December Futures.  At their highs, ES was up about 1.4% around 6:55 ET, and NQ was up about 2.4% around 9:50. Soon afterwards, those gains reversed quite abruptly.  The S&P 500 (SPX) gravitated once again toward the 7,300 level that has provided support over the past three sessions, while the Nasdaq 100 (NDX) spent very little time in negative territory.

ES December Futures, 2 Days, 2 Minute Candles

NQ December Futures, 2 Days, 2 Minute Candles

The pre-market bounce was easy to explain.  A supersized deal reaffirmed, at least for now, enthusiasm for the artificial intelligence theme that has propelled stocks over the past four years.  There was also a belief that many investors were raising cash to participate in the new issue, so there was hope that those who did not receive their desired allocations would put money back to work in other stocks. 

The rationale for the quick drop is less apparent.  It seems to be merely the latest round of “sell the rally” behavior that has pervaded market activity this month.  Around 11:30 ET, NYSE decliners led advancers by roughly 3:1, and the technology sector was the only SPX sector showing gains.  Within SPX, there were more than 250 net decliners. 

OK, while I was typing, the IPO began trading and stocks took another leg lower – a big one!  I updated the charts above with data from shortly after noon ET.  The drop was quick, stunning, and meaningful.  It appears that traders were waiting for the deal to begin trading to unleash another bout of selling, and once SPX broke through its recent support, that led to another round of sharp declines.

As of 12:18 ET, NYSE decliners are leading by a 4:1 ratio and SPX has 424 net decliners among its 500 stocks.   All 11 SPX sectors are lower, with only energy showing a loss of less than 1%.  What started as a hopeful day for many has turned into a significant disappointment. 

Barring a major turnaround this afternoon, we are looking at the type of day that some view as ominous.  With higher highs and lower lows than the prior day, SPX and NDX are potentially forming outside reversals.  Who knows, though?  SPX has rallied about 50 points since I posted the graphs above.  Perhaps the second leg lower was the result of stop-loss orders that had little follow-through.  Buckle up for the volatility.

[i] I think you know what stock I’m referred to, but I’m not allowed to discuss it until the selling syndicate closes.

data.title: Nasdaq 100 Jumps Ahead Of Anthropic Debut
data.description:
US equity futures are pointing higher across the board, with the Nasdaq 100 leading the advance with a 2% rise, as semiconductor stocks benefit from renewed enthusiasm around artificial intelligence. The index found decent support ahead of Anthropic’s (ANT) debut, with Nvidia (NVDA)’s earnings results also helping to stabilise sentiment. The recovery is certainly a welcome development after a troubling week for financial markets, with equities, gold, silver and Bitcoin (BTC.X) all coming under significant selling pressure.

So, is this an early sign that risk appetite is returning, or are we simply seeing a temporary rebound in the Nasdaq 100 futures within a broader bearish market? I think it is far too early for the bulls to declare victory until we see a more convincing sign of a market bottom.

All eyes on Anthropic

Anthropic has priced its shares at $83, raising $81.3 billion in what is reportedly the largest IPO on record. The stock is due to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT, with the company carrying a valuation of approximately $1.5 trillion.

Its sheer size is expected to put it on course for accelerated inclusion in several major indices, including the Nasdaq 100, as early as late November or December. That could generate substantial demand from passive funds tracking those benchmarks. The S&P 500, however, is likely to be a longer wait, given its eligibility requirements, including a sufficient period of public trading and sustained GAAP profitability.

The IPO provides another focal point for a technology sector that has struggled to maintain its earlier momentum.  Will Anthropic be among the biggest stock gainers today, or will it get sold?

US equities have weathered the storm for now, but choppy waters ahead

US equities have endured a difficult few sessions, yet their resilience remains striking when compared with the much steeper declines in Bitcoin, silver and several major Asian equity markets. That said, relative outperformance should not be confused with immunity to a broader correction. Despite today’s bounce, the Nasdaq 100 remains well below its October peak, while underlying vulnerabilities are becoming increasingly difficult to overlook.

There are several reasons why Wall Street has held up better than other markets. Unlike in 2022, when aggressive Federal Reserve tightening triggered a widespread repricing of risk, the US economy has remained relatively resilient. Corporate earnings have also provided a degree of protection, while the enormous investment flowing into AI infrastructure continues to support expectations for future growth.

Nvidia’s latest results have helped reinforce that narrative, easing concerns that the AI investment cycle might be approaching a turning point. But questions over the eventual returns on such substantial capital expenditure have not gone away. With valuations elevated, even modest disappointments in corporate guidance could prompt a more meaningful reassessment of the sector.

Monetary policy presents another potential headwind. Further evidence of persistent inflation could strengthen expectations of additional Fed tightening, pushing Treasury yields higher and making expensive equity valuations harder to justify.

For now, economic resilience, earnings growth and the AI investment boom are providing Wall Street with important support. Anthropic’s debut may offer a fresh catalyst for technology shares, but it does little to resolve the broader questions surrounding valuations and the sustainability of AI-related spending. The risk of a deeper correction should not be dismissed.

Nasdaq 100 technical analysis

The Nasdaq 100 was attempting to end a four-day losing streak, gaining more than 2% at the time of writing.

For now, I would approach this recovery with a degree of caution. Markets have been particularly choppy of late, and several major indices have already broken through important technical levels. The Nasdaq 100, for instance, has moved below its 200-day moving average recently, as you can see on the chart.

On the upside, initial resistance comes in between 27,850 and 28,230. This is an important technical area where several previous support and resistance levels converge, alongside the 200-day moving average and a short-term bearish trend line.

A decisive move back above this zone would be an encouraging bullish signal, potentially opening the door to further technical buying towards the 28,815 to 29,000 support-turned-resistance area. That is the next significant resistance zone, and a break above it would considerably improve the technical outlook.

On the downside, initial support is seen around 27,500, which marks Tuesday’s high.

Below there, we have 27,200. This is particularly important as it marks the late-July low, which was temporarily breached on a couple of occasions in early November and again earlier this week before the index recovered.

If the Nasdaq falls back below 27,200 and starts holding beneath that level, the technical picture would deteriorate considerably, increasing the risk of another leg lower.

Further down, the next major support zone comes in between 26,350 and 26,400, marking previous highs from late last year and early this year. This zone was tested earlier this month, providing a solid bounce.

So, has the market bottomed?

Potentially, but I wouldn’t jump on the bullish bandwagon just yet. We need to see further evidence before becoming confident that a sustainable bottom is in place. Until then, I would treat this as a level-to-level market, with the next few sessions potentially providing more clarity. Judging by price action elsewhere in financial markets, I would be extra careful to chase the market higher.

data.title: Scotia Metals’ Lithium Ambition: The Mine Builders Behind a New Exploration Story
data.description:
Dallas, United States, November 19th, 2026, FinanceWire


Disseminated on behalf of the issuer; Scotia Metals Corp.

After helping advance lithium operations and companies that became part of multibillion-dollar transactions, Scotia’s leadership is now pursuing two early-stage discovery opportunities as industry forecasts point to an urgent need for new supply.

Scotia Metals Corp. (CSE: SMET) (OTCQB: CSRVF) (FSE: C6R0) has secured an option to acquire the Nordestina lithium project in Bahia, Brazil, while advancing its inaugural drilling campaign at Acadia in Nova Scotia. But the broader reason Scotia could attract attention is the identity of the people building the Company: executives whose careers include major lithium mine developments, financings and resource specific mergers and acquisitions.

For early-stage exploration companies, drilling and assays determine geological prospects. Yet the ability to recognize opportunities, evaluate technical results, secure capital and eventually execute a project is also consequential. Scotia’s leadership has worked across several important chapters of the hard-rock lithium industry. Now it is building a new project portfolio before either Scotia property has established a mineral resource.

The Management Connection: Experience Built at Scale

Chairman Brian Talbot has more than 25 years of lithium operating and development experience, according to Scotia’s corporate profile. He held senior operating responsibilities at Galaxy Resources, including work at the Mt Cattlin operation in Australia, and served as chief operating officer of Sigma Lithium (Nasdaq: SGML) (TSX-V: SGML), overseeing commissioning of the Grota do Cirilo operation in Brazil. Scotia reports that Sigma reached approximately US$4.8 billion in market capitalization during his tenure. That is a historical valuation of Sigma, not a return earned by Scotia shareholders.

Director Nick Rowley was Galaxy’s director of corporate development and played a role in its merger with Orocobre, which created Allkem. Allkem later combined with Livent to form Arcadium Lithium, acquired by Rio Tinto (NYSE: RIO) in 2025 for approximately US$6.7 billion. Rowley also has experience with lithium project financing and offtake arrangements through RTEK International. These transactions illustrate the scale of businesses with which Scotia directors have been associated, not value created solely by any one individual.

CEO Rodrigo Roso brings roughly two decades of legal, M&A and project-development experience, including work involving Sigma Lithium and other mining businesses. Scotia director Shawn Khunkhun previously led Dolly Varden Silver which merged with Contango ORE, Inc. to create Contango Silver & Gold Inc. (NYSE: CTGO), a North American mid-tier precious metals producer and developer. Together, the team gives the company experience spanning exploration-stage strategy, operations, corporate development and capital markets.

The intriguing question is whether that experience can help Scotia efficiently identify and advance an economic lithium asset. The answer will depend on exploration results, financing, permitting and many other factors. Prior success at different companies does not predict a comparable outcome at Scotia.

Nordestina: Expanding Scotia’s Search Into Brazil

The Nordestina option adds a 16,566-hectare property comprising nine mineral permits in northeastern Bahia, Brazil, alongside Scotia’s Canadian flagship. Field crews have visually identified suspected spodumene at roughly 100 locations over an approximately 3.3-kilometer corridor. A total of 1,355 rock and soil samples were submitted for laboratory analysis, with initial assays anticipated in late November under the company’s stated schedule. Visual observations are preliminary and do not establish lithium grade, tonnage or an economic deposit.

The agreement allows Scotia to evaluate the property before committing the full acquisition price. It calls for US$10,000 monthly payments and reimbursement of up to US$210,000 in prior RTEK exploration expenses, with a US$2 million purchase price payable only upon exercise. Scotia has no minimum exploration spending requirement, can terminate on 30 days’ notice, and has until May 31, 2028 to exercise. This flexible structure may be especially relevant to an exploration-stage company deciding how to allocate capital across multiple targets.

Acadia: A Drilling Catalyst Already Underway

At Acadia, Scotia began a six-hole program of approximately 1,000 meters on November 9, targeting a possible bedrock source of spodumene-bearing boulder trains. The Company has documented five boulder trains spread across roughly 3 by 1 kilometers. Historical selected samples have graded up to 3.40% lithium oxide (Li₂O), and 20 of 38 channel samples from the recent program exceeded 1.0% Li₂O. These are surface and selected sample results, not drill intersections or an established resource.

The next meaningful step is to establish what, if anything, lies in bedrock beneath or near these surface indicators. Favorable results could guide additional work and raise the technical significance of the project; unsuccessful holes would require the exploration thesis to be reassessed. Full results were expected during the first quarter of 2027 under Scotia’s previously announced timeline.

The Supply Challenge: 134 New Mines and More Than US$100 Billion

The strategic backdrop is substantial. In October 2026, Benchmark Mineral Intelligence projected global lithium demand of approximately 7 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) annually by 2050, versus 2.11 million tonnes in 2026. Under its assumptions, that incremental demand is equivalent to production from 134 new lithium mines averaging 36,000 tonnes LCE per year. Expressed another way, the world would need to add the equivalent of a new mine about every two months for 24 years, requiring more than US$100 billion of investment. Benchmark’s upside-demand scenario points to more than 180 equivalent new mines.

The International Energy Agency’s 2026 outlook separately projects lithium demand to quadruple by 2040 and mined output to increase approximately 2.5-fold. Its assessment also indicates that anticipated projects may leave lithium supply deficits through 2035. These are scenario-based forecasts rather than guaranteed shortages; recycling, new technology, commodity prices and policy can materially change the outcome.

This creates an industry-wide tension: forecast demand may be enormous, but discovering a deposit is only the first stage. Successful new mines require teams capable of technical assessment, financing, permitting, construction, commissioning and commercialization. That is why Scotia’s management history is a relevant part of its story, even before any resource has been defined.

Why Scotia Deserves a Place on the Exploration Watchlist

Scotia’s case rests on a combination of management experience and identifiable upcoming technical events, not on a claim that a mine already exists. Nordestina offers a new potential target with pending laboratory data and limited immediate acquisition commitments. Acadia offers a drilling program intended to test the source of compelling but still preliminary surface indicators. If exploration delivers positive evidence, Scotia could have more information with which to plan follow-up programs and assess future development pathways.

A leadership team with experience at Galaxy, Sigma and other lithium businesses gives the opportunity a distinctive dimension: the people assessing Scotia’s early-stage properties have participated in building and advancing far more mature operations. Whether they can replicate any element of that trajectory here remains uncertain. For investors following the long-term supply buildout in lithium, the combination of experienced operators and near-term exploration results makes Scotia a company to monitor closely, with the risks inherent in junior mineral exploration fully in view.

data.title: Nvidia Doubled Revenue. P/E Fell To A 10-Year Low
data.description:
"Our momentum is real," Colette Kress said on 17 November, in her first results release as Nvidia's (NVDA) interim CEO. The figures backed her up. Revenue more than doubled in a year, to $115.8 billion, and the forecast for the current quarter came in above what analysts expected. The next day the shares fell 2.9%.

That is Nvidia's puzzle right now. The company earns more every quarter, and the market pays less for each dollar of it. At the 18 November close Nvidia traded at its lowest multiple of earnings in at least ten years. The report itself explains a good part of why.

Rubin's record start

In the three months to 25 October, Nvidia sold nearly twice as much as in all of fiscal 2024. Data center sales, the chips, networking and systems that train and run AI models, came to $107.6 billion of it, up 110%.

Much of the jump came from Vera Rubin, the rack-scale system that began shipping in the quarter. Kress told analysts it brought in nearly $20 billion in its first quarter, the fastest ramp in Nvidia's history. Networking, the gear that links thousands of chips into one machine, passed $21 billion.

The rest of Nvidia, now reported as Edge Computing, grew 42% to $8.2 billion on workstations and chips for robots and cars, while higher memory prices weighed on gaming PCs.

Nvidia revenue by customer

Nvidia splits its data center sales by customer, and the split tells a new story. Sales to hyperscale customers, the giant cloud and internet platforms, rose 71% to $60.1 billion. Sales to everyone else, a group of AI clouds, industrial companies and enterprises, nearly tripled to $47.5 billion.

A year ago that second group was under a third of data center sales. Now it is 44%. A longer customer list spreads Nvidia's risk, and it also brings in buyers with far less cash of their own than Microsoft or Amazon, the AI cloud start-ups above all.

How the buildout gets paid for

Those newer buyers need money, and Nvidia increasingly provides the backing. Its $32 billion of agreements with neoclouds, the young AI cloud companies, depend on those partners raising financing. It has also agreed to guarantee up to $105 billion of credit support for SB Energy's campus in Ohio, which will host Nvidia systems under 20-year leases to OpenAI.

Customers are paying more slowly, too. Money owed to Nvidia for chips already delivered rose to $81 billion, and the average customer now takes 64 days to pay, up from 60 a quarter earlier. Nvidia puts part of that down to longer payment terms on large multi-quarter deals with some investment-grade customers.

The cash still pours in. Free cash flow nearly doubled, and Nvidia returned a record $28.1 billion to shareholders, $22.1 billion of it through buybacks.

Nvidia's biggest customers already lean on borrowing, as we wrote in Nvidia's Biggest Customers Keep Spending. Power and Debt Set the Limits. Now the supplier stands behind part of the bill as well.

Why Nvidia stock fell after earnings

Then the price went the other way. Nvidia's earnings per share over the last four quarters rose 130% on a year earlier. Over the same year the share price fell 17%, and at the 18 November close it sat 37% below its record on 6 October.

Put those two together and the multiple collapses. Nvidia traded at 16x its trailing earnings, below every month-end reading of the past ten years. The low before this was 18x, in December 2018, and the ten-year median is 54x.

Two things explain much of the latest drop. The first sits at the top. Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and ran it from the start, resigned as CEO on 12 November, and the filing gave no reason. Kress runs the company until the board names a successor, Harvey Jones became its first chair, and an independent board committee is still investigating. On the earnings call the board ruled out bringing Huang back. From the last close before the news, the shares lost 13%.

The second is the forecast. The quarter to January has an extra week, so per week $130 billion is only about 4% above this quarter's pace, by our arithmetic, after 20% growth from the quarter before.

The forecast excludes data center compute revenue from China, compared with $2.4 billion of shipments there this quarter, and gross margin is guided down to 71% to 72% as Rubin ramps. Kress still expects revenue to grow about 75% next fiscal year.

How much Nvidia is in the S&P 500 and other ETFs

Most investors own Nvidia through a fund, and how much they own depends on which one. It is about 6% of both SPY, the S&P 500 fund, and QQQ, the Nasdaq-100 fund. Growth and tech funds hold more: about 10% of VUG, Vanguard's growth fund, and 14% of VGT, its tech fund.

Of these funds, the biggest share sits in SMH, VanEck's chip fund, at 17%. SOXX, the iShares chip fund, holds about 7%, because its index caps the weight of its largest companies.

That share is the lever. With everything else unchanged, a 10% move in Nvidia moves SPY by about 0.6% and SMH by about 1.7%.

The P/E here is the share price over the last four quarters of reported earnings per share; the fund shares are our look-through of each fund's holdings at the 18 November close.

Kress called the momentum real, and the report agrees. What the market will pay for it has not been this low in ten years.

data.title: Silver Investors Should Watch The Vaults, Not Just The Price
data.description:
Silver has slipped below $45 an ounce, yet the big vaults in London and New York have not been filling up, which means the fall is not coming from a surplus of metal, and the supply case for owning silver still stands.

If silver were piling up unsold, the big warehouses would usually show it. They do not. London held less silver at the end of October than a month earlier, the first fall in six months. In New York, the metal ready for delivery against futures barely moved while the price dropped. And India, the world's biggest silver consumer, spent nearly three times as much on silver imports in October as in September. On the stockpiles alone, that is a small positive for silver holders, based on one month of data. It is not a sign of a squeeze, and the next test starts on November 30.

Silver traded near $44.93 an ounce late on November 18. It was down about 5% on the day. Hawkish minutes from the Federal Reserve's last meeting added to bets on a December rate rise. The gold-silver ratio stood near 83, meaning one ounce of gold buys about 83 ounces of silver. Silver is now about 37% below its 2025 close. The latest premium issue at Golden Meadow® found the inventory picture calmer than the price.

There are six Deep Dives in this issue of the premium Silver Catalyst newsletter, and in this article, I'll focus on one of them.

 

London: The First Fall in Six Months

London is the centre of the world's wholesale silver trade, where large bars are stored. At the end of October its vaults held 28,889 tonnes, about 928.8 million ounces (Moz), according to the LBMA's monthly data. That is about 3.1 Moz less than at the end of September, after five monthly rises in a row.

A fall in London's stock is a change in where silver sits, not a measure of silver used up. Some of it may have gone to India, some to exchange-traded funds, which hold silver for investors and trade like shares, and some elsewhere. The LBMA does not say.

The vaults are well stocked but not full. They hold about 21% less than at their June 2021 peak. Metals Focus, a research firm, put the metal available outside those funds at about 267 Moz. Kitco reported the estimate alongside end-September vault data. That is nearly double the 136 Moz of London stock outside funds at the end of September 2025. Metals Focus and the Silver Institute called that a "record (reported) low", and it came weeks before London's October squeeze, when buyers struggled to find metal there. The two figures come from different reports and may not cover exactly the same metal. The 267 Moz figure also predates October's data, so the two cannot be combined to work out a new balance.

Funds may also have drawn on that metal. The iShares Silver Trust, which keeps most of its metal in London, added about 11 Moz from the end of September to November 10. If that metal came out of London's stock, the silver not held by funds fell by more than London's reported total did. That is my inference, because the LBMA does not split its figures by owner.

New York: Steady Through the Sell-Off

COMEX is the main US futures exchange, where traders agree a price today for silver delivered later. Its "registered" silver is metal with a warrant, a receipt that makes it ready for delivery. Registered stock stood at 101.63 Moz on November 9, on the exchange's own report. On November 18 it was about 101.2 Moz, on CME Group figures compiled by MetalCharts. The price fell hard over those nine days, and the deliverable metal hardly changed.

Open interest is the number of futures contracts still open. Counted in ounces, it came to about 5.7 for each registered ounce, the same ratio as a week earlier. Money managers, mostly hedge funds, held net bullish bets of 3,615 contracts on November 10. That is their bets on a rise minus their bets on a fall, and it is close to their lowest since February 2024.

So far fewer of these traders are betting on a rise than earlier in the year. The figure does not show how much forced selling is left, though. Large bets in both directions sit inside that small net number and cancel each other out.

Sources: LBMA, October and September 2026 vault data | LBMA, June 2021 record | CME Group, COMEX silver stocks, November 9 | MetalCharts, COMEX silver stocks from CME Group data, November 18 | CFTC, COMEX silver open interest and managed money, November 3 and 10 | Kitco, Metals Focus on London and positioning, October 29 | KNN India, citing Reuters, October 23 | India's Ministry of Commerce and Industry, September and October trade data, via Kitco and The Pamphlet | World Silver Survey 2026, Metals Focus and the Silver Institute

The open-interest ratio pairs the CFTC's November 10 figure with registered stock on November 18. The Kitco report carrying the 267 Moz figure does not give its date; it appears beside end-September vault data. The managed-money figures are longs minus shorts in the CFTC's disaggregated report. India's monthly trade release gives values, not tonnes.

 

India: The Buyer Came Back

India is the world's biggest silver consumer and imports most of what it uses. Dealers told Reuters that in late October the government issued permits to import about 6,500 tonnes over six months. That is about 209 Moz. It comes to roughly nine-tenths of India's imports in all of 2025, which Metals Focus and the Silver Institute put at 232.2 Moz.

A permit is a ceiling, not an order. When the permits were issued, Indian buyers were paying only 45 cents an ounce over official domestic prices. That points to a market that was not short of metal that week.

The first trade figures since then are firmer. India's commerce ministry put October silver imports at $1.91 billion. That is nearly three times September's figure. These are values, not volumes, and the price moved between the two months. October was still about 28% below October 2025, when India was buying heavily during the squeeze in London. November's figures, due in mid-December, will be the first full month under the new permits.

 

What This Means to Silver Investors

The stockpiles tell a different story from the price. A price that falls because there is too much silver around tends to leave metal sitting in vaults. In October, London's stock fell and India's imports rose. Into mid-November, New York's deliverable stock held. On one month of data, that is a small positive for the case that the world uses more silver than it produces.

It is not evidence of a shortage you can see yet. London is well stocked, nothing in New York showed strain, and India's buying came after months of curbs. Market reports blame the price fall largely on expectations of a December rate rise and a firmer dollar.

In their interim review on November 12, Metals Focus and the Silver Institute still forecast a sixth annual shortfall in a row, of about 35 Moz. That is smaller than the 46.3 Moz they expected in April. They also said that fund selling and the smaller shortfall have helped ease tightness this year in the physical market, where bars and coins change hands.

The next tests come quickly. November 30 is the first day buyers holding December contracts can be told their metal is ready for delivery. December is one of COMEX's main delivery months. A smooth month with registered stock near 100 Moz would confirm the calm. The LBMA's November figures follow around December 7, and India's November imports in mid-December. Stockpiles are one of the forces I follow in Silver Rising, and I keep track of how silver has traded against them.

data.title: Questions About Fed Rate Hikes Nobody Is Asking
data.description:
Gold and silver took it on the chin again on Wednesday. Gold fell below $3,750, and silver crashed through $46.

Why?

Fed people said some stuff.

The Federal Reserve released the minutes from the October meeting on Wednesday. Unsurprisingly, it reflected significant hawkishness among the committee members.

The minutes described inflation pressure as “broad-based,” and the committee essentially promised future rate hikes.

“Almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective.”

During an interview aired by CNBC, Fed governor Christopher Waller doubled down on the hawkish talk. Apparently, he doesn’t share Kevin Warsh’s aversion to “forward guidance.”

Waller said inflation is “heading in the wrong direction and is spreading out,” emphasizing that we can't blame every rising price on the oil shock. He insisted, "If you really want to get it down, you've got to start taking aggressive actions," hinting at a 50-basis-point rate hike in December.

So, there ya go! Rate hikes are locked in. Sell your gold and silver. Interest rates will remain higher for longer.

Will they, though?

Tunnel Vision

Before examining the assumptions more deeply, I have a more fundamental question.

Are we obsessing too much about what the Federal Reserve might do without thinking through all the possible ramifications?

The markets seem to have tunnel vision right now. All they can see is “the Fed hiking rates” and “interest rates higher for longer.”

News Gold Letter publisher Brien Lundin said the markets seem to have developed an “obsession” with Federal Reserve monetary policy.

“While it has always been an important factor in market analysis, it has grown to be the all-important consideration ever since the Great Financial Crisis. Like suckling piglets fighting for access to their mother’s milk, traders have been blinded to anything else in their investment decisions.”

He also pointed out that their addiction to easy money has made the markets “tolerant to the drug of monetary adrenaline, while also heightening their response to any indication of potentially hawkish policies.”

Lundin thinks this obsession has caused a bad case of tunnel vision, and mainstream market analysts are missing the big picture as they fixate on interest rates.

“What both the Fed and traders are ignoring, of course, are the long-term implications of higher interest rates.”

In other words, policies have consequences, and they aren’t always the ones you hope for or expect.

The Questions Nobody’s Asking

Everybody just assumes the Fed will hike rates and then hold them higher until inflation comes down. They also assume that it will work.

That’s debatable.

In the first place, what makes people think a modest 25-basis-point rate hike will slay inflation that has been above the 2 percent target for 68 months? Do you remember how much easy money central banks and governments created during the pandemic? Do you remember money creation during the Great Recession?

When the Fed launched quantitative easing (QE) in 2008, Ben Bernanke insisted it was a “temporary” emergency measure. He swore the Fed would only hold those bonds on its balance sheet for a short time. He promised that the Fed wasn’t monetizing the debt.

Nearly 20 years later, the balance sheet is multiple times larger than when Ben made his promise.

When Paul Volcker tackled inflation in 1980, he quickly jacked rates up to 20 percent. I’m not suggesting the Fed would need to hike that high to drive down the current wave of inflation. However, it’s fair to question whether 5 or 6 percent interest rates are adequate for the job.

In that sense, I agree with the central bankers' rhetoric. Inflation is high. Inflation is persistent. The central bank needs to act.

Which kind of makes you wonder: why haven’t they done more? It’s not like the central bankers haven’t had time. It’s been over five and a half years since CPI was at 2 percent.

And why is the Fed running inflationary QE operations right now, even as the committee members fret about too much inflation?

I’ll tell you why.

The massive debt black hole.

Mainstream analysis tends to avoid this issue like a stinky dog. They just tell us, “The Fed will hike!” and move along without considering what might happen when it does. I guess they assume that inflation will come down and the economy will march merrily along.

They might be right.

But they probably aren’t.

Economies buried in debt and addicted to easy money don’t fare well in a higher-interest-rate environment. The Fed people won’t say it out loud, but they know it’s true. They must be aware that if they keep hiking, they will collapse the debt-riddled bubble economy.

As already noted, most of that inflation generated during the Great Recession and the pandemic remains in the system.  The malinvestments and resource misallocations inherent in easy-money eras were never cleaned out. We’ve enjoyed an easy money boom for nearly two decades. Do you know what comes after a boom?

A bust.

We’re due.

Rate hikes may well be the pin that finally pops the bubble.  

You might want to think this through before you dump your gold and silver just because “rates are going up.”
